metrics: efficiency: Percent Optimized (OPT@k, at least 10% faster and correct) and Speedup Rate (SP@k) [execution; 25 runs, first run excluded]; correctness: pass private tests, NC rate [execution]
benchmarks: PIE (from CodeNet): Python test 986, C++ test 994; GPT-4 run on a 10% random sample of the test set
models: CodeLlama-34b-Instruct (open, code-specialized instruct); Gemini-pro (closed); gpt-3.5-turbo-0613 (closed instruct); gpt-4-1106-preview (closed instruct)
baselines: Instruction prompting, ICL (4 random shots), RAG (BM25), CoT; ablations
effect_target_headline: SP@5 on Python with GPT-4: SBLLM 209.59 vs COT 178.34; 'outperforming all baselines by 8.75% ∼ 28.06% and 1.15% ∼ 9.56%' top-5 speedup on Python and C++
effect_correctness_headline: baseline methods generate at least 27.18% incorrect code for Python. In contrast, SBLLM reduces this rate by 17.18% (ChatGPT top-1)
notes: Eligibility is borderline: this is LLM optimization of human-written slow code (PIE), which could be classed as adjacent/EC4. Here it is included because the LLM generates new code whose efficiency is measured. A Wilcoxon test against baselines is reported. The GPT-4 evaluation uses only 10% of the test set. Contamination is only argued in the threats-to-validity section. No call or token cost is reported, even though the method needs 5 samples x up to 4 iterations. Some table values (e.g., GPT-4 C++ OPT values such as 5.49, which are not multiples of 1/90) look odd and may have been garbled in extraction.

title: CortexCompile: Harnessing Cortical-Inspired Architectures for Enhanced Multi-Agent NLP Code Synthesis
technique_name: CortexCompile (cortex-inspired multi-agent code synthesis with Task Orchestration Agent)
metrics: readability-maintainability: survey score 1-5 covering readability, usability and satisfaction (human, 50 participants); correctness: % error-free execution / bug counts
benchmarks: 5 custom game development tasks (Pacman, Snake, Chess, RTS, FPS)
models: GPT-4o mini fine-tuned agents (claimed 1-9B, closed); GPT-4o (closed) as baseline
baselines: GPT-4o without fine-tuning (monolithic)
effect_target_headline: On average, CortexCompile received scores above 4.5 across all tasks, while GPT-4o's scores ranged from 3.5 to 4.2.
effect_correctness_headline: in the FPS game, CortexCompile produced code that was 92% accurate, compared to GPT-4o's 82% accuracy
notes: Readability is reported only within aggregated survey scores; per-criterion values sit in figures that are not available in the text. 'Development time' measures generation time, not the efficiency of the generated code. Implementation claims are dubious (GPT-4o Mini described as 1-9B parameters, GPT-4o as 1.8T). There is no fine-tuning data, no statistics and no artifacts. Eligibility is borderline; a reviewer should verify.

title: Measuring Code Efficiency Optimization Capabilities with ACEOB
technique_name: Fine-tuning on ACEOB efficient-inefficient pairs + NPI filter (cost-model reranking of beam/sampled candidates)
metrics: efficiency: NPI (normalized execution-time index; execution / cost-model based), IOCCB (similarity-to-reference to efficient codes); correctness: I/O pass rate (Pass@1)
benchmarks: ACEOB test set, 9,305 pairs, 289 problems (Codeforces, temporal split after May 4 2022)
models: CodeT5-small 60M open; CodeT5-base 220M open; CodeT5-large-ntp-py 770M open code; CodeGen-mono 350M open code; PolyCoder 0.4B open code; ChatGPT-3.5 closed instruct (no filter)
baselines: greedy, beam 5/10, sampling 5/10 without filter; ChatGPT
effect_target_headline: PolyCoder S10 NPI 47.84 vs S10+NPI 72.05; CodeT5-small S10 57.29 vs S10+NPI 84.74
effect_correctness_headline: CodeT5-small B10 I/O 0.46% vs B10+NPI 0.19%
notes: Efficiency metrics are custom: NPI may be based on cost-model predictions rather than measured runtime, given near-zero I/O pass rates; verify this. The text says 'PolyCoder B5+NPI ... 72.05', but the table shows 72.05 for S10+NPI. No baseline without fine-tuning is reported. Datasets are said to be released, but no URL is given. Tables are garbled.

technique_name: Prototype2Code (design linting + UI layout tree + GNN element typing + structured GPT-4 prompt for CSS)

effect_correctness_headline: SSIM 0.91 ± 0.07 vs CodeFun 0.64 ± 0.06 and Screenshot-to-code 0.58 ± 0.12
notes: LLM role limited to CSS style generation; eligibility is borderline. The readability difference is not significant; the maintainability difference is significant only vs Screenshot-to-code (p=0.02), not vs CodeFun (p=0.54). Table 3 appears garbled: the Screenshot-to-code PSNR value repeats its SSIM value (0.58 ± 0.12). Venue metadata saying 'Computability in Europe' is wrong; the paper is ASME IDETC/CIE 2024.

notes: Per-CWE tables (4, 5, 10–16) are garbled in the extraction; aggregate totals were taken from the text and from Table 6. Pass@10 for CodeGen-350M dropped slightly (9.9 base to 8.4); InCoder rose (27.7 to 29.4). Contamination was handled by filtering synthetic data with more than 75% token overlap with benchmark prompts. Artifact repository was announced as 'will be available'. A secondary result shows CodeQL report plus hint raises the GPT-4 repair rate to 83.99% on average.

technique_name: PromSec (gGAN-guided iterative prompt optimization)

Fig. 15 ablation shows CWE count 4 for PromSec vs 164/46 for ablations, but the bars are garbled. Functionality is mostly measured by a graph-similarity proxy. The pipeline also edits existing code, making it partly a repair setting, but the code is regenerated by the LLM.

notes: The security metric is a custom detector of outdated/vulnerable API usage, not a standard SAST tool. The benchmark is self-built, and each prompt was run 10 times, but no variance is reported. Table V is garbled, and one cell reports w/ 0.4861 for CodeLlama with an 85.11% reduction rate, which is inconsistent. The paper only says code will be open-sourced; no URL is given.

Each experiment was run 3 times with distinct seeds and averaged, but no variance is reported. Correctness is shown only in figures; the paper says it is mostly preserved, with slight reductions in some cases. Other headline results: 12.07% average security increase over the no-technique LM, and 7.74% on attacked models. Some table layouts in the extracted text are garbled.

title: Large Language Model Unlearning for Source Code
technique_name: PROD (Probabilistic Redistribution for Output Distribution) unlearning
metrics: security: forget quality = average of (1-BLEU vs vulnerable snippet [similarity-to-reference]) and CyberSecEval static analyzer pass rate [tool-static]; combined with utility via Pareto Dominance Ratio (PDR); human/GPT-4 pairwise perceptual win rate [human, llm-judge]
benchmarks: CyberSecEval (Purple Llama) insecure code autocomplete, 1,916 snippets, 50 CWEs; also copyrighted code (100 Stack files) and deprecated API (VersiCode-derived, 3,449 snippets); HumanEval for utility
models: CodeLlama-7B, open, code-specialized; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, open, code-specialized; DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, open, code-specialized; StarCoder-7B, open, code-specialized
baselines: Gradient Ascent, DPO, NPO, FLAT; original model
effect_target_headline: Insecurity PDR: Ours 70.4 vs NPO 24.5 (CodeLlama-7B)
notes: Security is one of three unlearning tasks. The forget metric mixes BLEU with static-analyzer pass rate, and the security results are reported mainly as PDR and plots, not as raw vulnerability rates. Only CodeLlama-7B was used for the security task; the other three models were tested on the copyright task only. Utility (HumanEval) is lower than the original model, so the correctness effect is a decline relative to no unlearning but better than the baselines. Results are averaged over 5 seeds but no variance is reported for the main results. The model was first fine-tuned on the forget data. Borderline fit to the review topic: removing memorized insecure snippets.

title: Beyond Local Code Optimization: Multi-Agent Reasoning for Software System Optimization
technique_name: Multi-agent whole-system optimization framework (component/behavior/environment summarization, analysis, optimization and performance evaluation agents)
metrics: efficiency: throughput (req/sec), average response time, P50/P90/P99 latency [execution, JMeter load test, 800,000 requests]; correctness: JUnit tests pass
benchmarks: TeaStore Java microservice application (6 services), single system
models: gpt-5.2 (closed)
baselines: Original unoptimized TeaStore
effect_target_headline: Throughput 1197.79 -> 1635.89 req/sec (+36.58%); Avg Response Time −27.81%
notes: Proof-of-concept: one system, one model, one run, no LLM baseline (comparisons with SysLLMatic, OpenCode and Codex are only planned). The LLM edits human-written code, so this is borderline with EC4/adjacent; it was included as LLM-generated performance edits. Correctness is stated as preserved via JUnit, but no numbers are given. Correctness and performance validation were run outside the automated pipeline.

title: CODMAS: A Dialectic Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework for Structured RTL Optimization
technique_name: CODMAS (Articulator + Hypothesis Partner dialectic agents, Domain-Specific Coding Agent with Domain Knowledge Injection, Code Evaluation Agent)
metrics: efficiency: critical path delay % improvement, power % reduction, area ratio A/A0 [tool-static synthesis, Yosys]; correctness: failure rate (syntax, functional or PPA failure) via testbench simulation [execution]
benchmarks: RTLOpt (new; 120 Verilog triples: 70 pipelining, 50 clock gating)
models: GPT-4o (closed); GPT-3.5-turbo (closed); DeepSeek-v2.5 (open); Llama-3 (open); Granite-34B-Code (open, code); CodeLlama-34B (open, code)
baselines: Zero-shot; CoDes, ReAct, Reflexion (prompting/agentic); LLM-VeriPPA; ablations w/o DA, w/o DKI, w/o CEA; shared-memory multi-agent (SMA) variant
effect_target_headline: Pipelining timing gain 25.5 (GPT-4o CODMAS) vs 15.4 LLM-VeriPPA; clock gating power 21.7 vs 9.3
effect_correctness_headline: FR 19.5 (GPT-4o pipelining CODMAS) vs 39.7 LLM-VeriPPA
notes: Hardware RTL PPA (delay, power, area) is mapped to efficiency; reviewers should check whether this fits scope. The input RTL is human-written and the LLM rewrites it, so this is optimization rather than generation from scratch. Prompts and temperature are not given. Statistical tests are claimed but the reported std values conflict (±1.2 in Table 6 vs ±0.6 in the text). No code URL is given. Table 2 is partly garbled: the human-reference row is misaligned and the ablation table columns are scrambled.

title: VeriAgent: A Tool-Integrated Multi-Agent System with Evolving Memory for PPA-Aware RTL Code Generation
technique_name: VeriAgent (Programmer/Correctness/PPA agents with evolving structured memory)
metrics: efficiency: critical path delay, area, power and Relative PPA Score = 1/(Delay×Area×Power) normalized to reference implementation [tool-static synthesis]; win rate vs. baselines
benchmarks: VerilogEval Machine/Human; RTLLM v1.1 (correctness); RTLLM v2.0 (PPA, ~44 designs)

baselines: Direct prompting; ChipSeek-R1; VeriPPA (results as reported in its paper); RTLCoder, BetterV, CodeV, OriGen, CraftRTL (correctness only); ablations

notes: The output is hardware RTL (Verilog), so PPA is treated as efficiency; this mapping is borderline, and the reviewer should check scope. No PPA number is reported for Direct prompting; the improvement is shown relative to reference designs and ChipSeek-R1. Many designs are N/A (no functionally correct, synthesizable design), so the geometric mean may be computed over different design subsets. No variance or repeated runs, no compute reporting, and no threats-to-validity section. The ablation lists 'w/o PPA Analyzer' in Table 3 but describes it as 'w/o PPA Agent' in the text.

effect_correctness_headline: RPR=0.60 vs 0.48 llm understand (GPT-5.2)
notes: The NF outcome is only an unnamed LLM-judge composite (CQ) with no validation; check whether this meets IC3. Tasks are LLM-generated from news articles and described as 'unseen'. There is no variance reporting. Datasets are only promised for release. Ablation tables are readable.

technique_name: POET (differential-testing testbench generation + power-oriented NSGA-II-style LLM evolutionary optimization)
metrics: efficiency: power (μW), area (μm²) and critical path delay (ns) from synthesis/STA [tool-static]; correctness: functional pass via simulation and equivalence checking

effect_correctness_headline: 100% functional correctness (40/40), compared to 72.5% for I/O prompting (29/40), 82.5% for CoT (33/40), and 90.0% for REvolution (36/40)
notes: Hardware RTL code. PPA is treated as efficiency. Optimizes expert-written designs, so this is borderline with the adjacent category. The paper states equal numbers of LLM calls across methods but gives no counts. Single run and single model. Table 1 is garbled in the extraction. Ablation results are reported as best-counts only. Prompts are not provided and the UCB exploration coefficient c is not given.

technique_name: EffiSkill (offline mining of Operator/Meta skills + execution-free diagnosis, skill retrieval, multi-plan composition, candidate generation)

notes: Input programs are human-written canonical solutions that the LLM optimizes; this is borderline with 'adjacent' (LLM editing of human code), but the LLM generates the evaluated code, so included. Correctness is folded into OPT@k and not reported separately. Prompts are not given in the text. Contamination is addressed only by a mining/eval overlap check. Figures 4-6 are garbled in extraction.

title: C2RustXW: Program-Structure-Aware C-to-Rust Translation via Program Analysis and LLM
technique_name: C2RustXW (structure-aware dependency-ordered translation + rule/LLM syntax repair + differential-testing semantic repair)

effect_correctness_headline: perfect SynCor across all projects and strong SemCor (78.87% on average)

Clippy warnings for C2RustXW are not always lower than the LLM baseline (PLTranslation). The abstract states 43.70% code-size reduction while the introduction states 49.60%.

Only a single model is used, which the threats section justifies by resources and contamination risk. Wilcoxon tests are reported for per-instance speedups on human-written code only. Table 3 extraction is partly garbled but the values are recoverable.

Correctness is checked only with LLM-generated tests, and the final output's correctness rate is not reported separately. Open-weight models largely failed because of tool-calling errors. Inference energy is estimated (~1.1 kWh overhead) rather than counted as calls or tokens.

No threats-to-validity section. The per-design PPA table is garbled in the extraction.

The 2026 date and the internally inconsistent software versions are suspicious and should be verified.

The 'training corpus' is claimed, yet the framework is also described as training-free. The input is compiler-generated assembly, not human-written code, which makes inclusion borderline (possible EC4/adjacent). Reviewer should check eligibility and data validity.

title: Improving Parallel Program Performance with LLM Optimizers via Agent-System Interfaces

metrics: efficiency: end-to-end throughput normalized to expert-written mappers (failed mappers scored 0), relative throughput vs OpenTuner [execution]; correctness: generation success rate (compiles and passes predefined tests) on 10 natural-language mapping strategies [execution]
benchmarks: 9 Legion benchmarks: Circuit, Stencil, Pennant, and six parallel matrix multiplication algorithms (Cannon's, SUMMA, PUMMA, Johnson's, Solomonik's, COSMA); 10 mapping strategies for DSL vs C++ generation ablation
models: gpt-4o-2024-08-06, closed, instruct
baselines: Expert-written mappers; random mappers (10 seeds); OpenTuner (RL autotuning with scalar feedback, 10 and 1000 iterations); OPRO; feedback ablations (0-shot, 5-shot, execution only, execution+explain); C++ code generation instead of DSL
effect_target_headline: Our approach finds mappers that surpass expert-written mappers by up to 1.34× speedup across nine benchmarks; With just 10 iterations, it outperforms OpenTuner even after 1000 iterations, achieving 3.8× faster performance
effect_correctness_headline: Success rate: C++ (single trial) 0%, DSL (single trial) 80%, C++ (iterative refine) 0%, DSL (iterative refine) 100%
notes: Headline 1.34x is the best mapper across 5 runs; mean normalized throughput over 5 runs is lower for several benchmarks (e.g. SUMMA 0.86x, PUMMA 0.57x, Solomonik 0.52x vs expert; Appendix A.4). Generated artifact is mapper code in a custom DSL compiled to C++. Single model (GPT-4o) without justification. Compute reported as iteration counts and ~10 minutes per application; no token/cost. No code URL and no threats-to-validity section. Year set to 2024 per record metadata; paper printed as ICML 2025 proceedings (arXiv v4 May 2025).

title: Multi-Programming Language Sandbox for LLMs
technique_name: MPLSandbox-driven self-correction (compiler feedback) and self-refinement (code smell analysis feedback)
metrics: readability-maintainability: average number of comment lines (tool-static, Radon raw analysis); cyclomatic complexity, Halstead volume, Maintainability Index shown only for one case-study instance (tool-static); correctness: Pass@1 (execution)
benchmarks: TACO (APPS+ and CodeContests portions plus newly crawled contest data); 12,000/1,000/1,000 train/validation/test problems; evaluated in 8 languages via system-prompt templates
models: GPT-4o, closed, general instruct
baselines: GPT-4o initial generated code before self-correction/self-refinement
effect_target_headline: Avg num of comment lines +8.9 (Python), +7.0 (Java), +7.2 (C++), +5.2 (C#), +5.6 (Go), +4.3 (Bash), +7.9 (JavaScript), +6.3 (TypeScript); GPT-4o after self-refinement (Table 3)
effect_correctness_headline: Pass@1 +3.7% (Python), +4.9% (Java), +2.7% (C++), +6.5% (C#), +5.0% (Go), +4.8% (Bash), +4.1% (JavaScript), +3.1% (TypeScript); GPT-4o after self-correction (Table 3)
notes: Primarily a tool paper. Metadata venue is ACL; the PDF itself says 'Preprint. Publication date: November 2024'. Other applications (Best-of-N verification, PPO with compiler-feedback reward on DeepSeek-Coder-Instruct-6.7B, unit test generation, code translation, vulnerability localization) are correctness-only or case demos and not extracted as NF techniques. Claims of lower complexity and better specification compliance after refinement are supported only by a single-instance example (Fig. 11: MI 59.24 -> 59.68, CC 7 -> 6); no aggregate complexity numbers. Number of refinement rounds not stated. Table 3 is a delta-only table with no absolute values; PPO results shown only in a figure without numbers. No threats-to-validity section.

models: GPT-4, closed; GPT-4-turbo, closed; Claude-3-Opus, closed; ERNIE-4.0, closed; LLaMA3-70B, open; PaLM-540B, closed; BLOOM-176B, open; CodeGemma-7B, open, code-specialized; StarCoder 2-15B, open, code-specialized; CodeQwen-14B, open, code-specialized; WizardCoder-15B, open, code-specialized; Code Llama-13B, open, code-specialized; OctoCoder-15.5B, open, code-specialized; CodeGeeX2-6B, open, code-specialized; CodeT5+-16B, open, code-specialized; CodeGen-16.1B, open, code-specialized; CodeX-12B, closed, code-specialized
baselines: Zero-shot; Few-Shot, CoT, Self-Edit, Self-Debugging, INTERVENOR, Self-Planning, CodeCoT, ReAct, Reflexion, RAP, ToT, CodeAgent, AgentCoder, ChatDev, AgentVerse, MetaGPT, Self-Collaboration (on GPT-4, PaLM-540B, Code Llama-13B); ablations of pool/retrieval/feedback
effect_target_headline: GPT-4 readability 85.6 (zero-shot) to 93.4 with CoP; "due to CoP's unique code-commenting mechanism, readability improved by 7.8 points"

Readability is the only NF dimension and is expert-rated without agreement; the commenting stage directly targets readability. The debugging loop relies on human expert feedback. Executability numbers for GPT-4 CoP differ between text (92.3 in Table 5, 92.4 in Table 6). Data available only on request. Limitations are mentioned only briefly in the conclusion.

title: C2SaferRust: Transforming C Projects Into Safer Rust With NeuroSymbolic Techniques
technique_name: C2SaferRust (C2Rust transpilation + static-analysis-based decomposition into translation units with call-site/dataflow context + LLM translation to safe Rust + compiler/test feedback repair)
metrics: security/idiomaticity: raw pointer declarations, raw pointer dereferences, lines of unsafe code, unsafe call expressions, unsafe type casts (tool-static, counts via compiler analysis; metrics from Laertes prior work); correctness: end-to-end test pass, translation success rate (execution)
benchmarks: 7 GNU coreutils programs (split, pwd, cat, truncate, uniq, tail, head) with end-to-end tests (new benchmark); 10 of 17 Laertes benchmarks (no tests)
models: gpt-4o-mini, closed, instruct
baselines: C2Rust output (no technique); Laertes; CROWN (CROWN ran on 4 of 10 programs); ablations: No Chunking, Random Order; variant with direct C-to-Rust translation
effect_target_headline: we are able to reduce the number of raw pointers by up to 38%, and reduce the amount of unsafe code by up to 28% (coreutils benchmark); C2SaferRust outperforms other approaches with a 39/2/9 aggregate win/tie/loss record over all 5 metrics (Laertes benchmark)
effect_correctness_headline: The resulting programs still pass all test cases.
notes: Venue taken from metadata (IEEE TSE); full text is arXiv v2 and does not state the venue. Input to the LLM is machine-transpiled (C2Rust) code from human-written C, so it is LLM translation/editing rather than pure refactoring of human code; reviewer may check EC4 borderline. Safety metrics are custom static counts of unsafe constructs, framed as both safety and idiomaticity; mapping to 'security' is approximate (no CWE/vulnerability scan). Tables 2-5 are heavily garbled in extraction. Correctness is maintained by construction (failed units reverted); per-baseline correctness not reported. Single model (gpt4o-mini), no repeated runs.

title: TPU-Gen: LLM-Driven Custom Tensor Processing Unit Generator
technique_name: TPU-Gen (prompt-template generator + LoRA fine-tuned LLM + RAG module retrieval + YOSYS/OpenROAD validation loop)
metrics: efficiency: power consumption, area, latency of synthesized designs vs PPA reference budget [execution/tool-static synthesis]; correctness: pass@k, pass/fail rates with testbench/manual verification [execution]
benchmarks: TPU-Gen dataset (25,000 TPU designs; v1 of 5,000 Verilog headers, 80:20 split); 30 designs for prompt-generator and RAG experiments; 4 DNN workloads (LeNet, ResNet18, VGG16, ResNet56) for PPA comparison
models: CodeLlama-7B-hf, open, code-specialized; CodeQwen1.5-7B, open, code-specialized; Mistral-7B, open, base; StarCoder2-7B, open, code-specialized; CodeLlama-13B (Q4), open, code-specialized; Claude 3.5 Sonnet, closed, instruct; ChatGPT-4o, closed, instruct; Gemini Advanced, closed, instruct
baselines: Manual optimization by an expert hardware designer (PPA); human input without prompt generator; fine-tuned models without RAG
effect_target_headline: average reduction in area and power of 92% and 96% from the manual optimization reference values
effect_correctness_headline: Models using RAG consistently achieved pass rates exceeding 95%, with Mistral-7B and CodeLlama-7B-hf attaining 100% success. In contrast, all models failed entirely without RAG
notes: Hardware (Verilog) generation; NF outcome is PPA of synthesized TPU designs, compared only against manual expert designs (Fig. 9, plotted, no per-workload numbers in text), not against a no-technique LLM baseline. The 92%/96% headline is stated in abstract/conclusion only. PPA largely depends on design parameters the LLM selects. Tables III-V garbled but readable. Dataset/models promised but link omitted.

title: A Preliminary Study on the Robustness of Code Generation by Large Language Models
technique_name: RobGen (line-level intervention checker + token-level conditional logit adjustment of the 'if' token)
metrics: robustness (defensive programming: input validation, boundary checks, error/exception handling): pairwise GPT-4o robustness comparison vs human reference, 1-5 scale, 3 repeats (llm-judge, validated against manual labels on 100 pairs, Cohen's kappa 0.81); AvgABE average atomic Boolean expressions (tool-static, Tree-sitter); EHAR exception-handling adoption rate (tool-static); correctness: Pass@1, Compile@1 (execution)
benchmarks: CoderEval Java, 230 repository-level tasks
models: DeepSeekCoder-1.3B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; DeepSeekCoder-6.7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; StarCoder2-7B, open, code-specialized
baselines: Greedy sampling (no technique); RobustCoder Prompt (robustness-instructing prompt); Post-Generation Insertion (FIM re-insertion of first-line 'if'); RobGen without checker (ablation)
effect_target_headline: RobGen reduces the proportion of less robust code by 10% (across five models); e.g., DeepSeekCoder-1.3B generated code underperforming human drops from 42.2% to 28.7%; average AvgABE 2.42 vs 1.65 greedy
effect_correctness_headline: achieves the highest average Pass@1 (43.57) vs 42.09 for greedy sampling
notes: Borderline on NF dimension: the target is 'robustness' (defensive programming: missing null/range/value checks, error handling), not explicitly security (no CWE/vulnerability scanner); mapped to security as input-validation-related; reviewer should decide whether robustness counts as an eligible NF dimension. The LLM judge was validated against manual comparison on 100 pairs (kappa 0.81) in the empirical part, and the open-coding of robustness patterns had kappa 0.71 between two authors. Judge scores averaged over 3 runs; runtime averaged over 3 runs on 20 tasks (RobGen +33.4% for DSC-1.3B, up to +197.9% for QWC-1.5B). Table 3 extraction is garbled but recoverable. Higher AvgABE is not monotonically better (StarCoder2-7B w/o checker 7.76 = redundant ifs).

title: MaintainCoder: Maintainable Code Generation Under Dynamic Requirements
technique_name: MaintainCoder (multi-agent pipeline: requirements analysis, design pattern selection, framework design + framework evaluation loop, code generation, code optimization with execution feedback)
metrics: readability-maintainability: Maintainability Index and Cyclomatic Complexity [tool-static]; dynamic maintainability via post-modification Pass@k [execution], AST similarity and code-diff (relative/absolute modified lines) between original and modified code [similarity-to-reference]; correctness: Pass@5 on original problems [execution]
benchmarks: MaintainBench (new): HumanEval-Dyn and MBPP-Dyn (30 problems each extended to 120 new problems), APPS-Dyn (50 problems extended to 200+), CodeContests-Dyn and xCodeEval-Dyn (30 each extended to 120+); 500+ problems total; plus original APPS, CodeContests, xCodeEval
models: GPT-4o-mini, closed, instruct; DeepSeek-V3, open, instruct; o3-mini, closed, reasoning (backbones); baselines also GPT-4o, Qwen-Plus, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Preview, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, GPT-4.1-mini (MetaGPT), all closed
baselines: Plain LLMs (GPT-4o-mini, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4o, Qwen-Plus, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Preview, Claude-3.5/3.7-Sonnet, o3-mini); CoT and Self-Planning prompting; AgentCoder, MapCoder, EvoMAC, MetaGPT; human competitive programmers
effect_target_headline: MaintainCoder(DeepSeek-V3) attains 36.7% Pass@5 accuracy (outperforming the second-best by +60%), 0.785 AST similarity, and the lowest relative code changes 33.0% (xCodeEval-Dyn); APPS-Dyn: MaintainCoder (GPT-4o-mini) MI 69.5 vs 63.3, CC 2.75 vs 5.10 for GPT-4o-mini
effect_correctness_headline: MaintainCoder (GPT-4o-mini) achieves an 11% increase on xCodeEval (from 46% to 57%), which is over double the improvement seen on APPS (44% to 48%)
notes: Tables 1, 2, 7, 8 garbled in extraction (columns split); headline numbers taken from running text and reconstructed rows. On entry-level sets static MI is not consistently better (e.g. MBPP-Dyn MaintainCoder DeepSeek-V3 MI appears lower than baselines), so static gains are strongest on mixture/competition levels; authors argue static metrics are inconsistent. Dynamic metrics are newly proposed and use a fixed Phase II generator (GPT-4o-mini; Gemini robustness check). Results averaged over five rounds but no variance or significance tests. No dedicated limitations/threats section. Human programmers used as a baseline, not as raters.

title: Smart contract generation model based on code annotation and AST-LSTM tuning
technique_name: Annotation-prompted instruction dataset with AST-LSTM+Transformer defect filtering and clustering, used for LoRA / P-Tuning v2 fine-tuning of LLaMA2-7B (FTmodel1 / FTmodel2)
metrics: security: pass rate ('accuracy') of generated contracts under VaaS, Mythril and SmartCheck, counting incomplete/repeated code and failed detection as errors [tool-static]; BLEU-1..4 against reference code [similarity-to-reference]
benchmarks: Self-crawled Ethereum (Etherscan) verified contracts: 6,739 samples split into function/contract/interface/library layers; 50 generated contracts per layer evaluated; ERC20 contract generation comparison
models: LLaMA2-7B (open, base) fine-tuned with LoRA (FTmodel1) and P-Tuning v2 (FTmodel2); comparison on ERC20 BLEU only: ChatGPT 3.5 (closed), Code Llama (open, code-specialized), Gemini (closed)
baselines: Non-fine-tuned LLaMA2-7B; an existing LSTM-based smart contract generation experiment (SmartCheck, contract layer only); ChatGPT 3.5, Code Llama, Gemini for BLEU on ERC20
effect_target_headline: The data accuracy of the two models in the contract layer increased by 9.3% and 8.2% respectively (SmartCheck, vs existing experiment); improvement of 6% and 7% over the non-fine-tuned model (71.2%); abstract: code security is improved by about 9%
notes: Full text is the Research Square preprint (March 2024), while metadata gives Journal of Supercomputing 2025; reviewer should check for differences with the published version. Correctness only proxied by BLEU (similarity to reference), so correctness_measured set false. 'Accuracy' of security tools is loosely defined and mixes completeness with vulnerability detection; only 50 samples per layer; comparison with 'existing experiment' uses a different setting. Security results are mixed across layers/tools (e.g., FTmodel2 interface layer VaaS 73.2% vs non-fine-tuned 69.6%; gains generally positive). No variance, compute, or artifacts (data on request).

title: QiMeng-GEMM: Automatically Generating High-Performance Matrix Multiplication Code by Exploiting Large Language Models
technique_name: QiMeng-GEMM: meta-prompts (platform-agnostic optimization-primitive descriptions plus platform-specific hints from a hint repository) with iterative beam-search auto-tuning over primitive permutations
metrics: efficiency: GFLOPS (CPU) / TFLOPS (GPU) throughput (execution); development time vs human coders; correctness: functional correctness of generated code (execution), reported as share of correct search trails and in hint ablation
benchmarks: GEMM on square matrix dimensions typical of deep learning (256-4096 on C910 CPU; 512-16384 on RTX 4070 and A100), 7 sizes per platform, 3 platforms
models: GPT-4o, closed, instruct; Claude 3.5 Sonnet, closed, instruct; DeepSeek-Coder-V2 236B, open, code-specialized; Codestral-22B, open, code-specialized
baselines: vanilla prompt; Chain-of-Thought prompt; hand-optimized libraries OpenBLAS 0.3.27 and cuBLAS 12.1; junior and senior human coders (development cost)
effect_target_headline: Compared to vanilla prompts, our method achieves a performance enhancement of up to 113× (GPT-4o, C910 CPU, 113.67×); up to 9.65× on RTX 4070 and 3.92× on A100; 211% of OpenBLAS on RISC-V CPUs and 115% of cuBLAS on NVIDIA GPUs
notes: Tables garbled in extraction. Correctness is used as a pruning gate; only partial correctness reporting (19-of-25-style '76%' of search trails correct; hint ablation says without hints LLMs fail to generate correct warp/thread tiling and float4 code). Codestral-22B shows near-zero or slightly negative gains on GPUs (0.97-1.15x), so effect is not uniform across models. Beam width and max iterations not given; meta-prompt full text not provided (appendix referenced but absent). No variance or repeated runs. Development time comparison with human coders reported.

title: Raw Pointer Rewriting with LLMs for Translating C to Safer Rust
technique_name: PR2: decision-tree-based prompting for raw pointer lifting and statement refactoring, with code-change-analysis-guided compilation and test-case error repair
metrics: security (memory safety): number and percentage of eliminated local raw pointers and affected functions (tool-static, tree-sitter counting); correctness: compilation + project test pass as gate, human user study of semantic equivalence (human), LLM-synthesized tests on uncovered functions (execution)
benchmarks: 28 real-world C projects with test cases from the NOPCRAT evaluation set (437 to 136k LOC, 17 to 2,731 raw pointers)
models: gpt-4o-mini, size NR, closed, instruct (main); Claude-3.5-Sonnet, size NR, closed (top 10 projects); Deepseek-v3.2, open, instruct (top 10 projects)
baselines: LAERTES (rule-based raw pointer to reference rewriting); C2Rust output; ablations NT (no decision tree) and NCC (no code change analysis)
effect_target_headline: PR2 removes 2,255 raw pointers, compared to 506 by LAERTES (3.46× more); on average removes 18.57% of raw pointers and transforms 13.05% of functions into safer code
effect_correctness_headline: all volunteers confirmed the rewritten code preserved original semantics (200 sampled eliminations); in 59 total cases we found only 2 incorrect pointer rewrites, corresponding to a 96.61% correctness rate among inspected cases
notes: Input code is C2Rust-transpiled Rust (machine-generated, not human-written), edited by the LLM; NF outcome is memory safety measured as raw-pointer elimination counts (a proxy, not a vulnerability scanner). Borderline adjacent/EC4 if reviewers treat this as LLM refactoring of existing code. Limitations note rewritten code may have low readability (not measured). Tables 1-2 are column-garbled but totals are stated in text. Single deterministic run (temperature 0).

title: CUDA-LLM: LLMs Can Write Efficient CUDA Kernels
technique_name: Feature Search and Reinforcement (FSR): generate N candidate kernels, filter by compilation verifier and function validator, select fastest via GPU performance profiler, refine prompt with errors/history or performance hints, repeat to depth D
metrics: efficiency: kernel execution latency, speedup normalized to human-written CUDA baseline, 5 input sizes per task [execution]; correctness: compilation plus output within deviation of human-written CUDA results on test inputs [execution]
benchmarks: 20 CUDA kernel tasks from NVIDIA CUDA Samples, LeetGPU and KernelBench, each at 5 input sizes
models: DeepSeek-V3-0324 (open, general instruct)
baselines: Human-written CUDA kernels (speedup baseline); direct LLM generation pass@5 (correctness)
effect_target_headline: the automatically generated kernels can outperform general human-written code by a factor of up to 179× in execution speeds; average speedups of 104×, 102×, and 179× (Matrix Transpose, Dot Product, Monte Carlo Integration) on an RTX 3090 Ti GPU
effect_correctness_headline: under the CUDA-LLM FSR framework, the LLM successfully completed all predefined tasks on GTX 1660 SUPER GPU and RTX 3090 Ti GPU (20 tasks), whereas direct generation (pass@5) failed some tasks
notes: Figure 3 (per-task speedups) is heavily garbled in extraction; Table 1 correctness checkmarks garbled. Efficiency baseline is stated as human-written CUDA, but Sec 4.2.2 also says 'compared to directly generated CUDA kernels, FSR consistently improves execution efficiency' - ambiguity in what the baseline is; some tasks show speedups below 1x (e.g. 0.433x, 0.494x) at some sizes. N and D not reported; no repeated runs, cost, artifacts or threats. Single model (DeepSeek-V3-0324) with brief justification. KernelBench-derived tasks may raise contamination concerns, not discussed.

technique_name: AlphaEvolve (LLM-guided evolutionary code superoptimization with evaluator feedback)

Only mathematical results released (Colab); system code not released. Compute only described loosely (thousands of samples, ~100 compute-hours per evaluation possible). title: EvoVerilog: Large Langugage Model Assisted Evolution of Verilog Code

notes: Eligibility depends on counting hardware resource utilization (wires/cells) as efficiency. Resource results only on hard subsets under 100-sample setting and compared to 'original solutions' (unclear which model produced them); non-dominated designs are rare (0-1 per backbone). Table 4 is garbled; reduced counts appear to be machine-hard 14/38, 10/37, 14/47 and human-hard 13/53, 25/63, 29/73 for GPT-3.5/GPT-4o-mini/DeepSeek-V3. Synthesis tool for wire/cell counts not named. Table 1 marks the method open source but no URL is given. Cost reported as API price per token (Figure 4), not total spend. No threats-to-validity section; no repeated runs.

title: ChatHLS: Towards Systematic Design Automation and Optimization for High-Level Synthesis
technique_name: HLSTuner: QoR-aware directive tuning with a fine-tuned LLM (SFT on optimization CoT) and iterative QoR-feedback refinement

technique_name: Evolutionary kernel optimization with LLM ensemble, LLM soft-verification (compilation/memory/numerics verifiers), least-to-most in-context kernel archive and LLM-summarized profiling feedback (after error-summary-guided PyTorch-to-CUDA translation)
metrics: efficiency: speedup over PyTorch eager and torch.compile, mean runtime over 2000 runs after 25 warmup [execution]; correctness: fraction of correct proposals / translation success rate across multiple inputs, inits and seeds (atol/rtol 1e-5) [execution]; verifier accuracy [execution]
benchmarks: robust-kbench (new; 9 task classes, 8 forward + 4 backward = 12 optimization tasks: MNIST cross-entropy, conv-relu-pool, maxpool, linear, linear-relu, LayerNorm, ResNet block, Llama FFW, Llama RMSNorm); KernelBench v0 levels 1 and 2 (200 tasks, with contaminated/exploitable tasks filtered)
models: o3 (closed, reasoning); o4-mini (closed, reasoning; also verifier and translation model); Claude Sonnet 3.7 (closed, instruct); GPT-4.1 (closed, instruct); Gemini 2.5 Pro (closed, reasoning; in 5-model ensemble ablation)
baselines: PyTorch eager and torch.compile implementations; Kevin-32B (RL-fine-tuned QwQ-32B) best-of-40 and reported results; Qwen3-32B best-of-40; Claude-3.7-Sonnet best-of-40; best-of-N parallel sampling for translation; ablations without verifier, without profile info, single model, 1-best / 10-random context
effect_target_headline: achieving up to 2.5× speedup in the forward pass (robust-kbench, over PyTorch eager); KernelBench L1+L2: average speedup reduced from 3.13x to 1.49x after excluding contaminated tasks
effect_correctness_headline: verifier-assisted optimization increasing the proportion of valid kernels from 55-70% to 80-85% in forward passes; translation succeeds on 95% of KernelBench level 1 and level 2 tasks
notes: Per-task efficiency results are mixed: backward-pass gains modest and some kernels at or below 1x (Table 4 H100: MNIST CrossEntropy fwd 0.91x, CrossEntropy bwd 0.97x; LayerNorm 12.52x vs native but 0.18x vs torch.compile); kernels overfit to the optimization input shape for LayerNorm and Linear-ReLU. 'Contamination' in the paper means exploitable/flawed KernelBench tasks, not training-data leakage, so contamination_handled set to 'no' (a reviewer may prefer 'partial'). No repeated runs/seeds or statistical tests. Figures 4, 6, 7 are garbled in extraction; numbers taken from prose and Tables 4-5. Cost ~$4-5 per kernel and ~1.5-2 h on 4 GPUs reported. Memory-access checks are part of correctness verification, not reported as a security outcome.

title: Code once, Run Green: Automated Green Code Translation in Serverless Computing
technique_name: ReFaaS: LLM-based Python-to-Go translation pipeline (Chain-of-Thought with documentation, build-fix and test-alignment recovery steps), integrated into Fission
metrics: efficiency: energy per invocation (J), delta energy/CPU/memory/cold start vs original function, invocations to amortize translation energy [execution]; correctness: buildable %, tests passed %, validated % (all black-box tests pass) [execution]
benchmarks: 14 custom Python serverless functions (basic, data structures, API, syntactic sugar) collected from tutorials, AWS/Google docs, CodeNet-based and API-doc-based functions; 4 JSON test events per function
models: QwQ (reasoning, open); Qwen2.5-Coder 32B (open, code-specialized); Gemma3 27B (open, instruct); DeepSeek-R1 32B (open, reasoning distill)
baselines: Original Python function (energy); pipeline variants: Chain of Thought (temp 0.1), Creative-CoT (temp 0.8), Single-Shot (no recovery)
effect_target_headline: translated functions can reduce invocation energy by up to 70%, achieving net energy savings after approximately 3,000 to 5,000 invocations, depending on the LLM used
effect_correctness_headline: the Creative-CoT Qwen2.5-Coder and Single-Shot Gemma3 yield the best results with a 43 percent translation success rate
notes: Two-column PDF extraction is interleaved and Table 3 is garbled (model-to-configuration row mapping unclear). The 70% average energy reduction in Sec 3.2 comes from MANUAL Python-to-Go translations (Fig 1, p=0.03); per-model energy of the LLM-translated functions is not reported separately, and the amortization analysis (Fig 6) appears to combine translation cost with the Fig 1 savings range. Translation energy cost (5-14 Wh) also reported. Borderline on whether NF outcome is measured on LLM-generated code specifically. Short paper (~8 pages); limitations and four challenges discussed but no formal threats section.

title: ConCuR: Conciseness Makes State-of-the-Art Kernel Generation
technique_name: ConCuR data synthesis and conciseness-based curation plus LoRA supervised fine-tuning (yielding KernelCoder)
metrics: efficiency: speedup = T_Torch / T_kernel times the correctness indicator, measured by execution against torch eager; fast1 = fraction of tasks with speedup greater than 1; Gspeedup = geometric average of speedups [all execution]. Correctness: Exec, the execution correct rate, where generated kernel output must match the PyTorch reference in dimension and value on random input [execution]. Auxiliary: ARL, average reasoning length in tokens, proposed as a task-difficulty indicator
benchmarks: KernelBench Levels 1 and 2 (200 tasks total; the difficulty division in Table 4 sums to 37 easy + 114 medium + 49 hard = 200). Levels 3 and 4 were excluded as beyond current model capability. Training data: ConCuR, 4,892 curated examples drawn from 90,810 synthesized (PyTorch, CUDA kernel, CoT) triples over 18,162 KernelBook tasks, of which 9,789 tasks had at least one correct generation and 24,136 kernels were correct
models: KernelCoder, 32B, open, reasoning (LoRA fine-tune of QwQ-32B); data synthesized by Kevin-32B, 32B, open, reasoning. Baselines evaluated: DeepSeek-R1-0528 685B open reasoning (Triton and CUDA); DeepSeek-V3.1-Think 685B open reasoning; Qwen3-Coder-Plus 480B code-specialized; GPT-4o closed; Claude-4-Sonnet closed; QwQ-32B open reasoning; Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-32B open; Llama-3.3-70B open; AutoTriton 8B open fine-tuned; KernelLLM 8B open fine-tuned; Kevin 32B open RL-trained; AI CUDA Engineer with o1-preview and o1-high (pass@10 table only)
baselines: Base model QwQ-32B; frontier models (DeepSeek-R1-0528, DeepSeek-V3.1-Think, Qwen3-Coder-Plus, GPT-4o, Claude-4-Sonnet); prior fine-tuned kernel models (Kevin, KernelLLM, AutoTriton); and four data-curation ablations trained with identical settings: 5K-random, 5K-max (the s1 longest-reasoning method), 5K-min, 5K-speedup; plus a dataset-size ablation at 552 / 1105 / 2210 / 4892 samples
effect_target_headline: Pass@1 fast1 on KernelBench: KernelCoder (32B) 17.0 on Level 1 and 39.0 on Level 2, versus its base model QwQ-32B at 7.0 and 11.0, versus Kevin (32B) at 16.0 and 27.0, and versus DeepSeek-R1-0528 (CUDA, 685B) at 18.0 and 38.0. Pass@10 fast1: KernelCoder 32.0 (Level 1) and 68.0 (Level 2) versus QwQ-32B 12.0 and 46.0. Ablation (Table 3, pass@1 / pass@10 fast1): KernelCoder 17.0 / 32.0 on Level 1 and 39.0 / 68.0 on Level 2, versus 5K-random 9.0 / 21.0 and 24.0 / 55.0, 5K-max 7.0 / 17.0 and 27.0 / 50.0, 5K-min 10.0 / 23.0 and 26.0 / 55.0, 5K-speedup 8.0 / 21.0 and 21.0 / 56.0. However, on the difficulty split (Table 5, Gspeedup pass@10) KernelCoder reaches 1.319 / 0.831 / 0.410 on easy / medium / hard, below Qwen3-Coder-Plus at 1.468 / 1.152 / 0.741
effect_correctness_headline: Pass@1 Exec: KernelCoder 58.0 on Level 1 and 59.0 on Level 2, versus QwQ-32B 18.0 and 17.0, Kevin 50.0 and 46.0, DeepSeek-R1-0528 (CUDA) 52.0 and 55.0. Pass@10 Exec: KernelCoder 91.0 and 95.0, versus QwQ-32B 55.0 and 76.0, Kevin 86.0 and 90.0. Difficulty split Exec pass@10: KernelCoder 100.0 easy, 94.7 medium, 83.7 hard, the best of the five models compared
notes: Methodologically one of the stronger papers in this batch: detailed hyperparameters, the full inference prompt in Appendix C, four data-curation ablations trained under identical settings, a dataset-size ablation, a training-cost comparison table, and a reported Pearson correlation (r = -0.047, p < 0.01) for the speedup/reasoning-length relationship. Caveats for a human reviewer. (1) Tables 1 and 2 are badly garbled by PDF extraction: the model rows are separated from their numeric columns and in the Smaller-Scale block the fast1 columns carry only 7 values for 8 model rows, most plausibly because KernelLLM has no fast1 entry. The KernelCoder values quoted above were cross-validated against the ablation Table 3, which independently lists KernelCoder as 58.0 / 91.0 Exec and 17.0 / 32.0 fast1 on Level 1 and 59.0 / 95.0 Exec and 39.0 / 68.0 fast1 on Level 2, so the KernelCoder and base-model figures are reliable; other baselines' fast1 values should be re-checked against the original PDF. (2) Baselines are run in different target languages (some Triton, some CUDA), which the tables note but the comparison does not control for. (3) The headline 'state-of-the-art' claim rests on Exec and fast1; on the harder difficulty split the geometric mean speedup of KernelCoder is below Qwen3-Coder-Plus, and the paper's own Future Work concedes that generated kernels 'do not exhibit satisfactory performance (at least, better than Torch Eager)' across all models. (4) No threats-to-validity or limitations section. (5) Contamination is not discussed at all, despite training data (KernelBook PyTorch programs) and the evaluation benchmark (KernelBench) being drawn from closely related PyTorch program distributions. (6) The ConCuR dataset itself does not appear to have a release URL; only the KernelCoder model is linked. (7) Figures 2, 3 and 4 are rendered as scattered axis numbers in the extraction, so the distributional claims behind Observation 1 could not be verified from the text alone.

title: IntrinTrans: LLM-based Intrinsic Code Translator for RISC-V Vector
technique_name: IntrinTrans (Translator / Compilation Executor / Test Executor / Optimizer agents with compile-and-test repair loop and register-usage-and-speedup optimization loop with performance-based selection)
metrics: efficiency: speedup of translated code vs native expert-written RVV intrinsics, measured on hardware [execution]; correctness: test pass rate on VecIntrinBench tests [execution]; also an 'efficiency score' based on number of repair iterations (translation process efficiency, not code efficiency)
benchmarks: VecIntrinBench (50 function-level Arm Neon -> RVV tasks)
models: GPT-5 Codex, closed, code-specialized reasoning; Claude-Sonnet-4.5 (20250929), closed, reasoning enabled and disabled; Gemini 2.5 Pro, closed, reasoning; Grok 4 (0709), closed, reasoning; DeepSeek-V3.2 (Exp), open, reasoning enabled and disabled; DeepSeek-R1 (0528), open, reasoning; Qwen3 Coder Plus, closed, code-specialized
baselines: Same pipeline without the register-usage-and-speedup optimization feedback (translated-only); rule-based Neon2RVV; native expert-written RVV code as performance reference
effect_target_headline: compared to before the introduction of register-usage-and-speedup feedback, the performance of these tasks improved by an average of 9.19% to 34.87% (Table III); optimized speedup vs native 0.85x to 1.28x, exceeding the rule-based Neon2RVV (0.63x)
effect_correctness_headline: test pass rates of IntrinTrans's translations ranged from 47% to 100% based on different LLMs, while the pass rate of rule-based Neon2RVV is 52%
notes: Venue in metadata is CSCWD; the paper text itself does not state a venue (arXiv v3), so recorded as preprint. Table II lists 9 model configurations (7 models, two with reasoning on/off); abstract says pass rate 47%-100%. Text says 50 tasks but pass rates like 97.1%/94.1% imply a denominator of 34, worth checking. Figure 4 speedup distribution is garbled. Prompts not given. Code promised on acceptance. Correctness effect vs Neon2RVV is mixed across models (some models below 52%).

title: Project-Level C-to-Rust Translation via Pointer Knowledge Graphs
technique_name: PtrTrans (C-Rust Pointer Knowledge Graph-guided project-level C-to-Rust translation: KG construction, KG-guided unit-by-unit translation in dependency order, and KG-guided incremental error correction)
metrics: readability-maintainability (idiomaticity): Lint Alert Count from Rust-Clippy, broken down into style, complexity, correctness and performance lints [tool-static]; security (memory safety): Unsafe Usage Count from Cargo-geiger (unsafe fn declarations, unsafe {} blocks, raw pointer dereferences) [tool-static]; correctness: %Compiled = compiledFunc/translatedFunc and %Equiv. = equivalentFunc/translatedFunc on manually constructed unit tests [execution]; case study: DSR@k and CodeBLEU for manual fixing effort [human / similarity-to-reference]; efficiency: runtime of four correctly translated Rust projects vs their C versions [execution]
benchmarks: 16 real-world C projects from the Crown dataset (avl, buffer, genann, quadtree, rgba, urlparser, ht, bst, json.h, libtree, binn, bzip2, heman, libzahl, lil, lodepng), up to 14,829 LOC; unit tests built with LLM-generated harnesses plus AFL++ fuzzing achieve 80.0-97.7% line coverage and 87.7-100.0% function coverage
models: ChatGPT-4o, closed, default backbone (temperature = 0); Claude-3.7-Sonnet, closed; Gemini-3-Pro, closed (both used for the generalization study)
baselines: Crown (rule-based ownership-guided rewriting of c2rust output); PR2 (LLM-based rewriting of c2rust output); FLOURINE (fuzzing-enhanced LLM translation, bottom-up order, Restart repair strategy, same backbone LLM); ablations PtrTrans_PS (no pointer semantics, i.e. the conventional bottom-up call-graph paradigm), PtrTrans_PU (no pointer-usage information), PtrTrans_RA (no Rust-oriented annotations), PtrTrans_EC (no error correction)
effect_target_headline: Across the 16 projects, PtrTrans reduces the Lint Alert Count by 94.9% compared to Crown (from 6,802 to 349) and by 91.6% compared to PR2 (from 4,135 to 349). Similarly, PtrTrans reduces the Unsafe Usage Count by 99.9% against both Crown (from 141,866 to 85) and PR2 (from 134,185 to 85). Wilcoxon signed-rank tests show both reductions are significant (p < 0.001); zero unsafe usages for projects under 4k LOC
effect_correctness_headline: For projects with LoC < 4K: average %Compiled 98.3 vs 69.9 and %Equiv. 81.6 vs 52.3 for FLOURINE (improvements of 28.4% and 29.3%); for 4K < LoC < 15K: %Compiled from 64.0% to 85.9% and functional equivalence from 14.2% to 67.9%. Ablation: %Equiv. rises from 59.5% (PtrTrans_PS) to 81.6% (PtrTrans) and from 50.8% (PtrTrans_EC) to 81.6%
notes: Two non-functional dimensions are targeted: idiomaticity/maintainability (Clippy alerts) and memory safety (unsafe usage). Efficiency is touched only in the threats-to-validity section: runtime of four correctly translated projects (avl, rgba, ht, bst) showed no degradation, with one figure given ('the translated Rust project runs 54% faster than the C version for the project bst'); no systematic efficiency evaluation. A human reviewer should check the fairness of the idiomaticity comparison: Crown and PR2 rewrite c2rust output for the whole project (hence enormous unsafe counts), while PtrTrans's counts are over its own translated project, which can contain unimplemented!() stubs for functions whose repair exhausted the five attempts (%Compiled below 100 for several projects). Record metadata gives year 2025 (arXiv v3 posted May 2026); the paper itself is Proc. ACM Softw. Eng. 3, FSE, Article FSE162, July 2026, which is what is recorded. Table 3 and Table 6/7 are heavily garbled by the PDF extraction (column blocks separated from headers); the totals cited here were cross-checked against the prose and the per-category totals (style 2790/3808/233, complexity 3945/269/94, correctness 58/58/10, performance 9/0/12). No compute or cost reporting; no contamination discussion.

title: TritonRL: Training LLMs to Think and Code Triton Without Cheating
technique_name: TritonRL: SFT distillation (DeepSeek-R1 or GPT-OSS 120B traces) + GRPO with Hierarchical Reward Decomposition (speedup reward on plan tokens, correctness reward on code tokens) gated by rule-based and LLM-judge validity verifiers
metrics: efficiency: fast1 and fast2 (share of tasks with a valid, correct kernel at least 1x / 2x faster than PyTorch reference) and mean speedup, pass@k, runtime averaged over 10 runs on NVIDIA L40S [execution]; correctness: valid (syntax + functionality via linter and LLM judge), compiled, correct (5 random inputs vs reference) [execution, tool-static, llm-judge]
benchmarks: KernelBench (Triton backend) Level 1 (100 single-kernel tasks) and Level 2 (100 fusion tasks); input-augmented KernelBench L1/L2 (500 evaluations per level)
models: Qwen3-8B, 8B, open, general/reasoning (base for TritonRL); Seed-Coder-8B-Reasoning, 8B, open, code-specialized reasoning (ablation base); teachers DeepSeek-R1, 685B, open, reasoning and GPT-OSS 120B, open, reasoning; compared Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B, KernelLLM 8B, AutoTriton 8B, Claude-3.7 closed
baselines: Qwen3-8B base (no fine-tuning); SFT-only checkpoints; KernelLLM; AutoTriton; Qwen3-14B/32B; Claude-3.7; DeepSeek-R1; GPT-OSS 120B; uniform-reward GRPO variants (beta 0.0-1.0); speedup-speedup reward assignment
effect_target_headline: KernelBench Level 1 pass@10: TritonRL (D) fast1 / fast2 36.0 / 13.0, mean speedup 1.10 vs Qwen3 (base) 8B 9.0 / 5.0, 0.41 and AutoTriton 25.0 / 10.0, 0.95; TritonRL (G) + IA 41.0 / 22.0, mean speedup 1.26
effect_correctness_headline: KernelBench Level 1 pass@10 compiled / correct: TritonRL (D) 100.0 / 78.0, TritonRL (G) + IA 100.0 / 88.0 vs Qwen3 (base) 99.0 / 23.0 and AutoTriton 92.0 / 57.0
notes: Code and datasets stated as 'will be available soon' (no URL). Training hardware given (8x A100 / 8x H200) but no training time, token or cost figures. No threats-to-validity section; only a short challenges paragraph. No discussion of overlap between KernelBook training tasks and KernelBench evaluation. Level 2 gains are smaller (TritonRL (G) + IA fast1 19.0 vs base 0.0). Tables partially garbled in extraction but values reconcile across Table 1 and Table 5.

title: From Large to Small: Transferring CUDA Optimization Expertise via Reasoning Graph
technique_name: ReGraphT / ReGraphT-MCGS: LLM-derived CUDA optimization reasoning graph retrieved step by step, explored with Monte Carlo Graph Search using compile/test/speedup rewards
metrics: efficiency: speedup@1 and speedup@10 over the sequential code (execution); correctness: pass@1, pass@10 (test-execution)
benchmarks: CUDAEval (new, 313 evaluation tasks: 106 easy, 105 medium, 102 hard, from Stack v2 CUDA files); ParEval CUDA subset (60 problems)
models: DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct (16B MoE, 2.4B active), open, code-specialized; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; HPC-Coder-V2, open, code-specialized (HPC fine-tuned); DeepSeek-V3-0324, open, instruct (reference); DeepSeek-R1, open, reasoning (reference and trajectory generator)
baselines: Standard prompting, Chain-of-Thought prompting, code-similarity RAG (CodeBERTScore retrieval over the same corpus), HPC-Coder-V2 fine-tuned model; large LLMs DeepSeek-V3/R1 as upper reference
effect_target_headline: achieving an average 2.33× speedup on CUDAEval and ParEval; CUDAEval speedup@1 for DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct: Standard 6.54 vs ReGraphT-MCGS 14.46
effect_correctness_headline: ReGraphT-MCGS achieves 73.3% in pass@k on average with three code-specific SLMs, surpassing by +11.0%, +9.0% and +6.8% compared to Standard, CoT and RAG in pass@1
notes: Table 1 is garbled in extraction (columns for Qwen2.5-Coder and HPC-Coder-V2 hard to align); headline 2.33x is the abstract's average claim. Speedup is relative to sequential C++ code, not to a CUDA reference. Wall-time overhead reported (about 6.02 h for 313 CUDAEval samples, search budget 100); ReGraph construction calls analysed. No repeated runs or statistical tests; no contamination discussion even though CUDAEval derives from Stack v2 and models may have seen it. Limitations section covers only benchmark coverage.

title: SwiftSolve: A Self-Iterative, Complexity-Aware Multi-Agent Framework for Competitive Programming
technique_name: SwiftSolve: Planner, deterministic Static Pruner, Coder, Profiler and Complexity Analyst agents with log-log complexity fitting and complexity-guided patch/replan loop
metrics: efficiency: TLE/MLE incidence (execution), runtime-vs-input-size curves (execution), success under contest time/memory limits (execution); EFF@k and complexity-fit accuracy defined but not numerically reported; correctness: PASS@1, Solved@<=k on hidden test harness (execution)
benchmarks: BigO(Bench) 16 tasks + Codeforces Div. 2 10 problems = 26 tasks x 3 seeds (78 runs)
models: Claude 4 Opus (Planner), closed, instruct/reasoning; GPT-4.1 (Coder and complexity fallback), closed, instruct
baselines: single-pass direct GPT-4.1; single-pass direct Claude 4 Opus
effect_target_headline: Against a Claude Opus 4 single-agent baseline, SwiftSolve improves run-level success (73.1% vs. 52.6%) at ~2× runtime overhead (12.4 s vs. 6.8 s); TLE/MLE failure rate 26.9% (SwiftSolve only)
effect_correctness_headline: PASS@1 = 61.54% (16/26) on the first attempt and SOLVED@≤3 = 80.77%
notes: Efficiency evidence is weak: EFF@k and complexity-fit accuracy are defined but never reported numerically; TLE/MLE rates reported only for SwiftSolve, not baselines; 'success' conflates correctness with passing resource limits. Baseline numbers given only approximately per dataset (GPT-4.1 ~60.4%/44.4%, Claude ~62.5%/46.7%); the 52.6% aggregate appears only in the abstract. Abstract runtime overhead refers to agent wall time, not program runtime. Small task set (26). Inconsistencies (intro says GPT-4.1 baseline; abstract says Claude Opus 4). Paper itself notes no ablations and no comparison with other multi-agent frameworks. 3 seeds but no variance reported.

title: The FM Agent
technique_name: FM Agent (expert-guided cold-start initialization + island-model evolutionary search with adaptive diversity-driven sampling + domain-specific evaluators, on a distributed Ray infrastructure)
metrics: efficiency: speedup of the generated CUDA kernel relative to torch.compile, measured by execution with 32 warmup and 128 profiling iterations (execution); kernel-level speedup against the official PyTorch implementation in the CosyVoice2-0.5B case study (execution). correctness (co-outcome): numerical tolerance tightened from 1e-2 to 1e-4 for acceptance, with reported accuracy maintained within 1e-5 (execution). Non-code benchmark outcomes also reported: MLE-Bench valid submission / above-median / medal rates and ALE-Bench performance scores (execution).
benchmarks: KernelBench Level 3, a clustered workload subset balancing coverage and diversity (exact task count not stated; Figure 6 shows roughly 13 kernels); additionally MLE-Bench (75 Kaggle competitions), ALE-Bench Lite (10 problems), three AlphaEvolve mathematical problems, and a CosyVoice2-0.5B Flow Matching Decoder case study (3 kernels)
models: Gemini-2.5-Pro, size undisclosed, closed, instruct/reasoning (used for FM Agent and for the OpenEvolve baseline in the controlled kernel comparison)
baselines: torch.compile (reference for kernel speedup); OpenEvolve powered by the same Gemini-2.5-Pro; AI CUDA Engineer (agentic SOTA); CUDA-L1 (RL SOTA); for the ablation: random sampling, top-k sampling, no cold start, no island model, and OpenEvolve
effect_target_headline: "Our approach achieves 2.08× to 20.77× speedups over torch.compile, consistently outperforming the previous SOTA reached while maintaining numerical accuracy within 10−5." (KernelBench Level 3 subset, Gemini-2.5-Pro, A100)
effect_correctness_headline: "maintaining numerical accuracy within 10−5"; acceptance tolerance tightened from 10−2 to 10−4; no per-task correctness or compilation rate is reported for KernelBench
notes: Only the KernelBench part of this multi-domain paper yields a non-functional outcome; MLE-Bench, ALE-Bench and the mathematical problems are task-score benchmarks, not code-quality measurements. The kernel evaluation is thin: the number of KernelBench Level-3 tasks in the constructed subset is never stated, the per-kernel speedup figure (Figure 6) has badly garbled x-axis labels in the PDF extraction, and only the 2.08x-20.77x range is given, with no per-kernel table, no variance and no correctness rate. Figures 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11 and 12 are extracted as label fragments only. The framework description is conceptual throughout (no pseudocode, prompts, hyperparameters or sampling formulas), and no code or data artifact is released for FM Agent (the linked repositories are baselines). Variance is reported for MLE-Bench (3 runs, SEM) and the ahc016 ablation (5 runs, standard deviation) but not for the kernel results. An optional human-in-the-loop module is described, but the authors state that for all three benchmarks optimization was performed exclusively by the LLM without human intervention. No threats-to-validity section and no contamination discussion.

title: PRAGMA: A Profiling-Reasoned Multi-Agent Framework for Automatic Kernel Optimization
technique_name: PRAGMA (profile-guided multi-agent kernel generation: Coder, Verifier, Profiler, Conductor agents with historical-best retention)
metrics: efficiency: speedup over Torch reference runtime and Fast1 (% correct and at least as fast as Torch) [execution]; correctness: success rate (compile, run, match reference outputs) [execution]
benchmarks: KernelBench (GPU and CPU backends; number of tasks not stated; six categories)
models: DeepSeek-R1, open, reasoning
baselines: Torch reference implementations; N-PRAGMA (PRAGMA without profiling feedback); Caesar (single-agent KernelBench multi-turn baseline, GPU only)
effect_target_headline: On the CPU, PRAGMA achieves an average of 2.81× speedup over Torch and 10.95× improvement over N-PRAGMA. On the GPU, PRAGMA delivers a 2.30× speedup over Torch and a 1.90× improvement compared with N-PRAGMA. (GPU Table I: Speedup 2.30 vs 1.28 N-PRAGMA vs 0.51 Caesar; Fast1 59.8% vs 32.2% vs 14.3%)
effect_correctness_headline: Success (%) on GPU: PRAGMA 92.0, N-PRAGMA 92.0, Caesar 49.0
notes: Short paper; single model (DeepSeek-R1), single run, no variance. CPU success rates not reported in a table; number of KernelBench tasks/levels used is not stated. Prompts not given in full. Abstract claims 'up to 10.95x' which is the CPU average over N-PRAGMA.

title: AccelOpt: A Self-Improving LLM Agentic System for AI Accelerator Kernel Optimization
technique_name: AccelOpt (three-agent planner/executor/summarizer workflow + beam search over candidate kernels + self-curated optimization memory of slow-fast kernel pairs)
metrics: efficiency: percentage of peak throughput computed from a roofline model (min required HBM traffic / bandwidth, matmul FLOPs / PeakMM, vector FLOPs / PeakVec) over measured latency; measured kernel latency in ms (warm-up iterations plus 10 repeated runs, up to 10 rounds, 1% (Trainium 1) / 4% (Trainium 2) difference threshold); speedup over the baseline kernel (geometric mean of per-task best speedup); cumulative Fast@p; traffic efficiency and tensor/vector/scalar engine utilization from the profiler [execution and profiler]; correctness: output compared against a CPU full-precision reference under several random seeds with a per-task tolerance [execution]; cost in US dollars from input+output token counts
benchmarks: NKIBench (new): 14 NKI kernels from real-world LLM workloads (AdamW, Add+RMSNorm+Matmul, BatchMatmul, BatchMatmul+Softmax, Group Query Attention, LoRA, Mamba block, Matmul+Add+RMSNorm, Matmul, RMSNorm+Matmul, RoPE, SiLU, SwiGLU, Transpose+Matmul), evaluated on Trainium 1 and Trainium 2; additionally 24 Triton kernels from FlashInfer-Bench on H100 and one Conv2D kernel from a Stanford CS149 assignment
models: gpt-oss-120b, open, reasoning (medium reasoning effort; planner/summarizer in the main setting and best executor in the cost study); gpt-oss-20b, open, reasoning; Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct-FP8, open, code-specialized instruct (executor in the main setting); Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct, open, code-specialized; Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507, open, reasoning; Claude Sonnet 4, closed, thinking mode enabled

Record metadata gives year 2025 and venue arXiv.org; the paper itself carries the MLSys 2026 proceedings header, which is what is recorded here. All figures (6, 7, 9-18) are images and their numbers could not be extracted, so the headline figures come from the abstract and prose; Tables 1-6 extracted readably. title: Translating Large-Scale C Repositories to Idiomatic Rust
technique_name: Rustine (preprocessing + automated C refactoring for unary operators, pointer arithmetic, constness maximization and large-function breakdown; dependence-graph-guided context and translation order; RAG-based API translation; two-tier LLM translation loop with compiler feedback and adaptive in-context-learning examples; test-based validation and delta-debugging-inspired repair)
metrics: security / memory safety: number of raw pointer declarations and dereferences, number of pointer arithmetic / comparison operations, number of unsafe lines, type casts and calls (all tool-static, via pycparser for C and the rustc_hir crate for Rust). readability-maintainability: idiomaticity = TSI x Clippy flags per KLoC where TSI = LoC_Rust / LoC_C and flags cover cargo, complexity, correctness, perf and suspicious lints (tool-static, Clippy); Cognitive Complexity, Halstead and SEI Maintainability Index (tool-static, rust-code-analysis); number of clippy::style violations (tool-static). correctness (co-outcome): percentage application- and test-code compilation success, and assertion pass rate from executing the translated test suites (execution). Also reported: translation time, dollar cost and token counts; human repair effort in hours.
benchmarks: 23 real-world C repositories taken from the artifacts of prior C-to-Rust work, 27 to 13,200 LoC (qsort, bst, rgba, quadtree, buffer, grabc, urlparser, xzoom, genann, ht, robotfindskitten, libcsv, avl-tree, libopenaptx, libtree, opl, libzahl, zopfli, snudown, lodepng, bzip2, binn, tulipindicator); test suites manually augmented to 1,221,192 assertions with average function and line coverage of 74.7% and 72.2%
models: DeepSeek-V3, size not stated, open-weight, instruct (base translator); DeepSeek-R1, size not stated, open-weight, reasoning (fallback after 8 failed attempts); OpenAI o4-mini, closed, reasoning (used only to synthesize adaptive in-context-learning examples)
baselines: C2Rust (rule-based transpiler), C2SaferRust, CROWN, Laertes, RustMamp, Syzygy; plus an internal ablation of Rustine with the pointer-arithmetic refactoring component removed
effect_target_headline: "the number of raw pointer declarations/derefenreces is reduced from 4,080/2,045 in C to 198/126 in Rust"; pointer arithmetic reduced by refactoring "from 452 to 14"; ablation without pointer-arithmetic refactoring: "the number of pointer arithmetic increases by 83.01%, raw pointer declarations/dereferences by 52.6%/154%, and unsafe ⟨lines,type casts,calls⟩ by ⟨64.42%, 31.67%, 61.46%⟩"; versus baselines, "C2Rust, C2SaferRust, CROWN, and Laertes have 4,904/20,169, 1,400/5,510, 3,027/12,298, and 2,255/9,685 more raw pointer declarations and dereferences"; unsafe ⟨lines,type casts,calls⟩ ⟨114, 47, 130⟩ for Rustine versus ⟨974, 70, 372⟩ for RustMamp, while "Syzygy translations contain no unsafe constructs, compared to 14 in Rustine translations"
effect_correctness_headline: "Rustine can generate fully compilable Rust code for all and achieve 87% functional equivalence (passing 1,063,099 assertions out of 1,221,192 in test suites with average function and line coverage of 74.7% and 72.2%)" — 100% compilation is fully automated, while the 87% assertion pass rate includes a human developer repairing semantic mismatches in 4.5 hours on average; 10 of 23 projects reached 100% functional equivalence with no human intervention
notes: Dimension mapping is a judgment call a human reviewer should confirm: the paper's 'safety' metrics (raw pointer declarations/dereferences, pointer arithmetic/comparisons, unsafe lines/casts/calls) are memory-safety proxies and were coded as the security dimension, while 'idiomaticity' (Clippy flags per normalized KLoC) and the three readability metrics were coded as readability-maintainability. Tables 1, 2 and 3 and Figures 6, 9, 10, 12, 13 and 14 are badly garbled by PDF extraction (column values appear as long interleaved runs of numbers), so only the aggregate figures quoted in the running text were copied; per-project values must be re-checked against the PDF. The paper also reports a human study, but it measures repair effort rather than rating code quality: one developer with over ten years of C and Rust experience and no familiarity with the subjects repaired the non-equivalent translations in 4.5 hours on average (min 0.33, max 10), with a strong size-effort correlation (rho = 0.86, p = 1.59e-4); there is a single annotator and no agreement statistic, which is why human_eval is coded 'none'. Statistical tests are reported only for effort/cost/time correlations, not for the quality metrics, and each project appears to be translated once with no repeated runs or variance. The reported 87% functional equivalence is not fully automated. Contamination of the open-source C subjects in the models' pretraining is never discussed. A_max and the block threshold theta_b are not given numerically (theta_f is 50% of the LLM context window). The authors note they recalculated several baselines' metrics after finding bugs or suppressed Clippy rules in those artifacts, which makes the baseline numbers theirs rather than as-published.

title: His2Trans: A Knowledge-Guided Agentic Framework for Project-Level C-to-Rust Migration
technique_name: His2Trans (historical C/Rust migration knowledge mining and retrieval at interface and fragment level, scaffold-constrained knowledge-guided function translation, then project-level agentic refinement with compilation, semantic and unsafe feedback)
metrics: security/memory-safety: Unsafe Ratio = fraction of Rust source lines inside or directly associated with unsafe constructs [tool-static]; correctness: Incremental Compilation Pass Rate (per-function body replay under a common scaffold) and Test Pass Rate on the project's own tests [execution]; all averaged per project then across projects
benchmarks: Two datasets: 10 OpenHarmony modules (161-3,544 LOC each, 1-14 files, 7-160 functions, 4-135 tests) and 8 open-source C projects used in prior C-to-Rust studies (urlparser, avl, ht, qsort, buffer, rgba, quadtree, genann)
models: DeepSeek V4 Pro, size NR, open-weight, instruct (main translation and refinement); Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, 32B, open, code-specialized (offline knowledge extraction only); Claude Code (general coding agent, underlying model not stated) as a baseline
baselines: C2Rust (rule-based transpilation); C2SaferRust (unsafe-reduction pipeline); EvoC2Rust; Tymcrat; Claude Code-only (general SE agent); plus an ablation: knowledge-guided translation alone, + compiler-driven per-function repair, + project-level agentic refinement
effect_target_headline: On ten OpenHarmony modules, His2Trans reaches a 100.00% incremental compilation pass rate, a 94.92% Test Pass Rate, and a 16.35% Unsafe Ratio. On eight open-source C projects, it reaches 100.00% for both incremental compilation and Test Pass Rate, reducing Unsafe Ratio from 42.88% under C2Rust to 8.59%
effect_correctness_headline: OpenHarmony averages: Test Pass Rate 94.92% (His2Trans) vs 80.08% (Claude Code-only), 67.50% (C2Rust), 40.92% (C2SaferRust), 0.00% (EvoC2Rust and Tymcrat); incremental compilation 100.00% vs 99.58% for C2Rust
notes: Unsafe Ratio is treated here as the security/memory-safety dimension; a reviewer who reads 'security' strictly as vulnerabilities/CWE may disagree, and unsafe ratio is also partly a maintainability/idiomaticity proxy. The effect direction is not uniformly positive against every baseline: on the open-source dataset Claude Code-only reaches a lower Unsafe Ratio (4.04% vs 8.59%) at equal compilation and test pass rates, which the authors attribute to Claude Code being free to abandon the C-compatible interface boundary; on OpenHarmony His2Trans is clearly better (16.35% vs 33.67%). Ablation on OpenHarmony: knowledge-guided translation alone 95.82% / 39.29% / 15.95% unsafe; + compiler-driven per-function repair 100.00% / 94.92% / 22.52%; + project-level refinement 100.00% / 94.92% / 16.35%, i.e. the refinement stage buys back unsafe reduction without changing test pass rate. The Unsafe Ratio instrument (how lines 'directly associated with' unsafe are counted) is defined only in prose, no tool named. Single translation model, no repeated runs or statistical tests, no token/cost/time reporting. Contamination: evaluated target modules are excluded from the retrieval pool and a threats paragraph acknowledges residual leakage from public mirrors and pretraining data. Tables IV and V are heavily garbled in extraction (per-project columns interleaved); the quoted numbers are taken from the abstract, prose and average rows, which are unambiguous. Venue metadata is empty; arXiv v4 (cs.SE), formatted as an IEEE conference submission.

No variance/statistical tests or compute/cost figures; ECA DMOJ ablations are single runs on few problems. Tables and figures heavily garbled in extraction (Table 1/5, Figures 5-8). Conflict of interest disclosed (Google DeepMind authors, Gemini models).

technique_name: Agent factory: Stage 1 per-sub-kernel optimizer agents (7 variants each) + agent-formulated ILP selection under area budget; Stage 2 N parallel exploration agents doing cross-function pragma/code/memory/compute optimizations (agent scaling N in {1,2,4,8,10})

GPT-5.2 best SOL-guided variant uses in-prompt form; uCUTLASS+SOL on GPT-5.2 (2.79x) does not exceed uCUTLASS alone (2.85x). No explicit threats-to-validity section.

title: Kernel-Smith: A Unified Recipe for Evolutionary Kernel Optimization

metrics: readability-maintainability (patch minimality / stable-context preservation on plausible patches): Average Edit Distance (character Levenshtein) [tool-static], Code Consistency Rate [tool-static], Average Total Changed Lines and Tokens [tool-static]; metrics validated by human preference study [human]; correctness: pass@1/5/10 via compilation and test suites [execution]
