CCR not uniformly improved (HumanEval-Java DS-Coder-6.7B CCR 71.4 under SFT vs 67.2 under PAFT). Percentages in tables are relative to Base, headline 32.6% AED reduction is relative to SFT. Contamination checked via SHA-256 of normalized snippets. Single run, no variance reported. Artifacts mentioned as released scripts/results but no URL in text.

title: ENCRUST: Encapsulated Substitution and Agentic Refinement on a Live Scaffold for Safe C-to-Rust Translation
technique_name: ENCRUST: ABI-preserving wrapper-pattern per-function translation with compile-test retry and rollback (Phase 1), type-directed wrapper elimination, and tool-equipped agentic refinement under a baseline-aware compile-and-test gate (Phase 2)
metrics: security (memory safety): raw pointer declarations, raw pointer dereferences, unsafe lines of code, unsafe type casts, unsafe call expressions (tool-static counts, metrics from C2SaferRust); readability-maintainability (idiomaticity): Clippy warning count (tool-static); correctness: test-script / test-vector pass rate (execution) and function compilance pass rate (compiler)
benchmarks: 7 GNU Coreutils programs (C2SaferRust benchmark; 65,117 LoC, 1,210 functions, 63 test scripts) and 8 of 10 Laertes libraries (132,589 LoC, 1,156 functions, 1,000 AFL++ inputs each); 197,706 LoC and 2,366 functions in total
models: GPT-4o, closed, general instruct (temperature 0.0)
baselines: C2Rust (rule-based transpiler output); C2SaferRust (with GPT-4o, temperature 0.0); EvoC2Rust (with GPT-4o, temperature 0.0); ablation Phase 1 only
effect_target_headline: Encrust reduces unsafe lines of code by 37.8% over the C2Rust baseline while achieving 100% test-vector correctness on all programs (15 programs); on Coreutils, reduces raw pointer dereferences by 55% and unsafe type casts by 60% relative to the C2Rust baseline
effect_correctness_headline: Function compilance pass rate 96.4% (Encrust) vs 66.0% (C2SaferRust) on Coreutils; Encrust achieves 100% correctness on all seven Coreutils programs and all eight Laertes libraries (EvoC2Rust 0%)
notes: Code translation (C to Rust) task; security dimension is operationalized as counts of unsafe Rust constructs (memory-safety proxy), not CWE/vulnerability scans. Clippy totals improve vs C2Rust and C2SaferRust (Coreutils 2,951 / 2,087 / 1,495; Laertes 7,174 / 7,034 / 6,453) but are worse than C2Rust for some libraries (genann 32 -> 59, lil 583 -> 698, qsort 7 -> 16, urlparser 153 -> 196), so the readability effect is mixed at program level. EvoC2Rust has lower nominal unsafe counts but does not compile (0% correctness). Correctness is 100% by construction (test-gated); EvoC2Rust safety numbers computed after substituting C2Rust bodies for missing functions. Only GPT-4o used, single deterministic run (temperature 0). Compute reported only as loop iterations (avg 21.0 per completed Phase 2 task); no tokens/cost. Laertes test vectors promised upon publication; no code URL. ACM template with placeholder venue/dates (Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 2018) - treated as preprint (arXiv 2604.04527v1). Tables are extracted as column streams but values are interpretable.

title: Record-Remix-Replay: Hierarchical GPU Kernel Optimization using Evolutionary Search
technique_name: Record-Remix-Replay (R3): LLM-ensemble MAP-Elites evolution of kernel source with record-replay evaluation, inner Bayesian optimization (TPE) over compiler pass pipelines and launch parameters, prefix-cache-aware prompting and runtime-aware LLM selection
metrics: efficiency: kernel speedup over baseline implementation, absolute kernel time, end-to-end application speedup, compute-time reduction [execution]; search cost: time-to-solution, evaluations per hour, GPU utilization; correctness used only as a filter (bitwise or annotated-tolerance replay check), not reported as an outcome
benchmarks: HeCBench CUDA/HIP versions of Lulesh (15 kernels), MiniFE (7), S3D (54), miniWeather (7 on data path); QUDA CoarseDslash kernel case study

notes: Main comparative results are given as box plots (Figs 6-9) without numeric tables; headline numbers come from the QUDA case study. Correctness is a hard filter (bitwise replay check; final kernels manually verified) rather than a reported rate. Only one LLM ensemble configuration; no per-model ablation of optimization quality. notes: Tables 1, 3, 4 and Figure 2/3 are garbled in extraction (cost/turn/token columns misaligned). Contamination considered via 'uncontaminated agentic baselines' (Atrex copies AITER reference kernel) and a DSL absent from training corpora; manual reward-hacking review. Ablation (flash attention): full Ave 588 TFLOPS vs 190/255/194 for ablated harnesses. Best-of-trials reporting; no variance across agent runs; limitations discussed in Discussion but no formal threats section.

title: Xe-Forge: Multi-Stage LLM-Powered Kernel Optimization for Intel GPU
technique_name: Xe-Forge: LLM-planned multi-stage optimization pipeline with Chain-of-Verification-and-Refinement (CoVeR) agents and Intel GPU knowledge base
metrics: efficiency: speedup and TFLOPS vs PyTorch eager, torch.compile and unoptimized Triton; geometric mean speedup; fraction of kernels improving; roofline placement [execution]

notes: Input kernels are LLM-generated (KernelFalcon) correct Triton code, which the LLM pipeline then rewrites; treated as LLM generation/editing rather than refactoring human code. Cost reported only as estimate (40-50 calls worst case, 10-20 typical, ~$0.50-$2.00 per kernel). Setup says full KernelBench suite across three levels but results reported only for 97 Level-2 kernels; Level-1 described as minimal gains without numbers. title: AdaExplore: Failure-Driven Adaptation and Diversity-Preserving Search for Efficient Kernel Generation

title: Beyond Correctness: Enhancing Architectural Reasoning in Code LLMs via Scalable Labeling with Agentic Judgment
technique_name: Agentic architectural judging pipeline for SFT data curation (Architecture Complexity Judge + Architecture Quality Judge with repository-specific generated rubrics), followed by supervised fine-tuning on the filtered trajectories
metrics: readability-maintainability (architectural conformance / structural quality): distribution of AQJ four-tier verdicts over all generated patches - High, High-with-concerns (HWC), Acceptable, Low - produced by a repository- and issue-specific rubric with priority-ordered axes and prose anchors [llm-judge]; the ACJ five-level complexity verdict (Trivial/Low/Moderate/High/Expert over five axes) is used for data selection, not as an outcome [llm-judge]. correctness: SWE-bench resolved rate under pass@1 (all specified unit tests pass on first attempt) [execution]; patch precision = resolved issues / patches generated [execution]. Convergent validity: Spearman correlation of the judge verdicts against 157 static architecture metrics [tool-static].
benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified (500 verified bug-fixing instances) and SWE-bench Multilingual (300 bug-fixing instances across 9 non-Python languages). Training pool: 5,000 high-quality Python trajectories from RepoForge, filtered to 3,360 architecturally curated instances; the metric-based filtering baseline yields 1,548 instances. Stated to have no overlap between training and evaluation data.
models: Fine-tuned: Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B (open-weights, instruct/reasoning). Teacher for trajectory generation: MiniMax-M2.5 (open-weights). Judge backbone: described only as 'a strong LLM' and never identified.
baselines: Original (base model, no fine-tuning); FullData (fine-tuned on the entire 5,000-trajectory pool, i.e. unfiltered SFT); Metrics (filtering by thresholded static architecture metrics, Qwen3-8B only); for the judge itself, random-forest prediction of ACJ/AQJ verdicts from 157 static metrics.
effect_target_headline: "our approach increases the proportion of architecturally conformant patches from 61-72% to 84-94% across model sizes" (abstract/introduction); per model, "For Qwen3-8B, the combined High+HWC proportion increases from 60.9% to 83.6%; for Qwen3-14B, from 64.0% to 87.1%; and for Qwen3-32B, from 72.1% to 93.5%." Versus the unfiltered FullData baseline the architectural quality is only comparable: "High+HWC proportions of 83.6% vs. 87.5% on Qwen3-8B, 87.1% vs. 83.9% on Qwen3-14B, and 93.5% vs. 93.3% on Qwen3-32B".
effect_correctness_headline: "Fine-tuning Qwen3-8B/14B/32B on 3,360 curated instances achieves resolved rates of up to 27.2% on SWE-bench Verified - up to 540% over the base model and 256% over unfiltered fine-tuning." Per model on SWE-bench Verified: 3.2% -> 17.4% (Qwen3-8B), 4.6% -> 17.8% (Qwen3-14B), 9.0% -> 27.2% (Qwen3-32B) versus Original; 6.8% -> 17.4%, 9.4% -> 17.8%, 15.6% -> 27.2% versus FullData. SWE-bench Multilingual: "our approach improves over the Original baseline by 286% - 420%" (1.4% -> 4.0%, 4.3% -> 9.7%, 3.3% -> 14%). Metric-based filtering baseline: 14.4% vs 17.4% on SWE-bench Verified and 4.7% vs 6.7% on Multilingual (Qwen3-8B).
notes: Main methodological concern for a reviewer: the architectural-quality outcome is measured by AQJ, the same author-built LLM judge that was used to select the training data, so the headline NF improvement is partly circular; the judge is never validated against human expert ratings (only against static metrics, where it deliberately does not correlate), and the LLM backbone powering the judges is nowhere identified. Against the unfiltered FullData baseline the architectural-conformance gain essentially disappears (83.6 vs 87.5, 87.1 vs 83.9, 93.5 vs 93.3), so the clear NF gain is only versus the untuned base model; the paper's distinctive claim versus FullData is about resolved rate and data efficiency, not conformance. Table 1 is hard to read because the AQJ columns are reported as relative changes to each model's own baseline while the baseline row is absolute, and the extraction garbles one cell ('17,1' for 17.1). Internal inconsistencies to check: the abstract says 286-424% cross-language improvement while Section 5.2 says 286-420%; Section 5.1 says 'improves the resolved rate by 174% - 256% compared to using the full dataset' where those figures are ratios rather than percentage improvements; Table 3's first row is labelled 'Original' with size 5,000 and value 6.8%, which is the FullData condition in Table 1, not the untuned base model; Table 3 lists SWE-Multi 5.0% for that row while Table 2 gives FullData Qwen3-8B as 3.0%. Tables 4 and 5 appear to have their captions swapped relative to their contents (the 'ACJ-style' table uses AQJ-correlated features). Results are single pass@1 runs with no variance, repeated runs or statistical tests, and no compute/cost figures despite the paper itself noting the token cost of agentic judging.

title: daVinci-kernel: Co-Evolving Skill Selection, Summarization, and Utilization via RL for GPU Kernel Optimization
technique_name: daVinci-kernel (SFT cold start on diversity-filtered data + joint multi-turn REINFORCE/TRLOO training of Skill Selection, Policy and Skill Summary agents sharing one backbone, with BM25+LLM skill retrieval injected at inference and execution-verified skill library updates)
metrics: efficiency: Fast_x = % of tasks with a functionally correct kernel achieving >= x speedup over the PyTorch reference, x in {1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0}, last-turn and best-turn (execution)
benchmarks: KernelBench Level 1, Level 2, Level 3 (task counts not stated)
models: Qwen3-8B-Base fine-tuned (daVinci-kernel-8B), open, base; Qwen3-14B-Base fine-tuned (daVinci-kernel-14B), open, base
baselines: GPT-5, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, DeepSeek-V3.2-Thinking, GLM-4.7 (zero-shot, from Dr. Kernel paper); Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B, AutoTriton; Cold-Start-8B/14B; Dr. Kernel-8B/14B (reported and reproduced); 5 ablations (no skill injection at inference, unfiltered SFT, policy-RL only, BM25-only selection, no skills)
effect_target_headline: daVinci-kernel-14B achieves 37.2%, 70.6%, and 32.2% on Level 1, Level 2, and Level 3 under the Fast1 threshold, outperforming the strongest prior RL-trained model, Dr. Kernel-14B (reproduced: 30.4, 58.5, 22.1); Fast1.2 at 14B improves Level 2 from 18.1 to 27.1 and Level 3 from 2.8 to 7.3
notes: Correctness is folded into Fast_x (a task counts only if the kernel is correct and faster); no separate correctness rate except 8-sample case studies (Task B: 8/8 vs Dr. Kernel 5/8). Some ablations beat the full method on individual cells (e.g., Ablation 5 Level 2 Fast1 51.6 vs 44.8 at 8B), so effect is mixed across thresholds/levels but positive overall vs Dr. Kernel. Baseline frontier-model numbers copied from the Dr. Kernel paper, not rerun. Single run per configuration, no variance. Training cost only as seconds per step (1734s vs 1466s). The case study's 2.0x speedup comes from skipping computation when min_value==0.0, which reviewers may view as a benchmark shortcut. Learning rate and several RL hyperparameters not given in text. Tables garbled but recoverable; only a brief limitations section, no threats-to-validity section.

title: Bridging Functional Correctness and Runtime Efficiency Gaps in LLM-Based Code Translation
technique_name: SwiftTrans: MpTranslator (parallel ICL with hierarchical-guidance fine-tuning on progressively accelerated translations) + DiffSelector (pairwise diff-aware LLM judge with ordinal-guidance training, bubble selection)
metrics: efficiency: Execution Time (ms, average over efficiency-critical inputs, 5 runs) and memory usage (MB) [execution]; maintainability: cyclomatic complexity [tool-static]; correctness: Computational Accuracy (%) [execution]
benchmarks: Extended CodeNet (200 x 5 languages), extended F2SBench (1000 x 5), new SwiftBench (500 x 5, problems from Jun-Oct 2025), each with 10 efficiency-critical test cases; ClassEval-T, AlphaTrans, RepoTrans (correctness only); 20 translation directions
models: Qwen2.5-3B, open, base/instruct; Qwen2.5-7B, open; StarCoder-7B, open, code-specialized; baselines Qwen3-Next-80B, open, instruct; GPT-5, closed, reasoning; data-construction ensemble DeepSeek-Coder-V2-16B, gpt-oss-20B, Qwen3-Coder-30B, open
baselines: Correctness-Only, Correctness+Efficiency, Correctness->Efficiency prompting on Qwen3-Next-80B and GPT-5; F2STrans (ICML 2025) on Qwen2.5-3B/7B; repeated sampling; ablations (w/o Lhg, w/o Dt, tgt0-only, tgtn-only, w/o Log, w/o diff, w/o Bi-Judge, all-pair vs bubble, list-wise selection)
effect_target_headline: Average Execution Time 292 ms (SwiftTrans, Qwen2.5-7B) vs 731 ms (F2STrans, Qwen2.5-7B) and 399 ms (GPT-5 Cor.->Eff.), Table 1 Avg. column
effect_correctness_headline: applying SWIFTTRANS to Qwen2.5-7B outperforms GPT-5 by 3.8% (average Computational Accuracy)
notes: Table 1 is garbled in extraction; headline ET averages (292 vs 731, 399) were read from the reconstructed Avg. column and should be verified. Additional dims: memory 23.9 MB vs 29.1 MB (F2STrans) and cyclomatic complexity 5.7 vs 7.0 (Table 4). Inference-only (no training) variant also reported (Table 11). Incorrect translations are assigned baseline runtime in ET. Benchmark test cases were annotated by three teams of 20 professionals (not a human evaluation of outputs). No code/data URL given; no threats-to-validity section. Stage could also be considered post-generation selection; training-time chosen because both components are fine-tuned.

title: SpecGen: Accelerating Agentic Kernel Optimization with Speculative Generation
technique_name: SpecGen: iteration-level speculative generation (non-reasoning forks conditioned on the reasoning prefix) with speedup-threshold early termination, plus ElasticScheduler (dynamic validation/profiling GPU split, LAF/FIFO priority queues, remote KV-cache for reasoning prefixes)
metrics: efficiency of generated code: best kernel speedup over the KernelBench PyTorch reference, averaged over 40 timed runs after 10 warmups, aggregated by geometric mean [execution]; system-level: end-to-end execution time, profiling feedback count, validation/profiling GPU utilization, token consumption [execution]
benchmarks: KernelBench: ten Level 1 tasks (T1-T10, HingeLoss and matmul variants) and ten Level 2/3 tasks (T11-T20), 100 iterations per task; workload characterization on the same ten Level 1 tasks
models: GLM-5.1, open, reasoning, served locally with vLLM on 8 GPUs; DeepSeek-V4-Pro, closed API, reasoning, high reasoning effort; temperature 0.1, reasoning disabled for speculative forks
baselines: CudaForge (Coder-Judge multi-agent with NCU feedback); AlphaEvolve (evolutionary coding agent); KernelAgent (Meta autonomous kernel generation); CudaForge+ with doubled token budget; internal ablations (speculative generation only, + reallocation, + priority queue, + remote prefix cache) and termination-criterion variants
effect_target_headline: improving 1.24–1.91× kernel speedup under a fixed time and token budget; geomean speedup over the reference reaches 5.78× on GLM-5.1 and 3.49× on DeepSeek-V4-Pro, geomean lifts of 1.24× over CudaForge, 1.91× over AlphaEvolve, and 1.52× over KernelAgent
notes: Primarily a systems-efficiency paper (end-to-end agent runtime, profiling feedback, GPU utilization); the in-scope NF outcome is the speedup of the generated kernels (Table 6, Table 8, Table 9). Correctness is enforced by the validation gate (compile, run, numerical match) but is not reported as a comparative outcome for SpecGen vs baselines; the per-iteration success/failure distribution in Figure 3 is characterization of the baseline framework only. No threats-to-validity or limitations section, no artifact URL, no contamination discussion. Variance control is 40 timed runs after 10 warmups per kernel; no repeated whole-run seeds or statistical tests. Several tables (Tables 4, 6, 8, 9) and figures are garbled in extraction; Table 8's T18 speedup column reads 0.35 vs 55.79, which looks anomalous and should be checked against the PDF.

title: EGG: An Expert-Guided Agent Framework for Kernel Generation
technique_name: EGG (expert-guided staged optimization: multi-seed search + algorithmic refinement + hardware-specific tuning [parallel mapping, tensor tiling, memory optimization] with stage-aware code/profile/debug multi-agent collaboration)
metrics: efficiency: mean speedup over PyTorch Eager, Fast1 rate (correct and faster than PyTorch Eager), latency in ms (execution); correctness: success rate (compiles and passes numerical correctness check) (execution)
benchmarks: KernelBench (250 tasks: Level 1 100, Level 2 100, Level 3 50); TritonBench real-world operators (3 tasks: Flash Attention, RoPE Embedding, INT8 Dequant MatMul); 25-task KernelBench subset for TVM Relax comparison
models: GPT-5.1, closed, general-purpose (main); Claude Opus 4.5, closed, general-purpose (KernelBench Level 2 only)
baselines: PyTorch Eager; Torch Compile (default and max-autotune); ChatGPT-5.1 and DeepSeek-V3.2 direct generation; AutoTriton (RL-fine-tuned); CudaForge (multi-agent with hardware feedback, re-evaluated under same setup); TVM Relax; handwritten TritonBench kernels; component ablations
effect_target_headline: 2.13× average speedup over PyTorch Eager on KernelBench (GPT-5.1, RTX 4090); Level 2: 2.73× vs CudaForge 2.00×
effect_correctness_headline: 100% success rate on all three KernelBench levels vs ChatGPT 5.1 60%/60%/66%
notes: Full prompts and pipeline pseudocode in appendix; no code URL given. Cost: ~20 min and ~50,000 output tokens per kernel vs CudaForge ~30 min and ~110,000. Second model (Opus 4.5) only on Level 2. No variance/repeated-run statistics. Limitations section (Appendix G) but no formal threats-to-validity. Ablation table rows garbled in extraction (full 87.6% Fast1 / 2.13×).

title: Decomposer: Learning to Decompile Symbolic Music to Programs
technique_name: DECOMPOSER: SFT (LoRA) on synthetic STRUDEL-SYNTH pairs followed by GDPO reinforcement learning with execution faithfulness reward (multi-instrument onset F1) and LLM-judged 12-item readability rubric reward
metrics: readability: 12-item binary readability rubric score (Rubric) [llm-judge] and average rank from listwise LLM reranker (Rank) [llm-judge]; diversity: SelfCB (CodeBLEU self-similarity) [similarity-to-reference]; correctness/faithfulness: compile rate [execution], Onset F1, Frame F1, multi-instrument Onset F1 of rendered MIDI vs input [execution]
benchmarks: STRUDEL-SYNTH test split (1,022 pairs); LMD short fragments <30 s (~1K test); generalization: LMD 30-60 s, GigaMIDI, NES-MDB, Nottingham (200 inputs each, Best@5); ModArchive genre benchmark (4,463 inputs, 51 genres)
models: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, 4B, open, instruct; Qwen3-8B, 8B, open, instruct/hybrid-reasoning (thinking disabled)
baselines: Vanilla Qwen3-4B/8B; SFT-only; RL without SFT; readability-weight sweep (w2 = 0 to 1.0); frontier LLMs prompted (Claude-Opus-4.6, Gemini-3.5-Flash, GPT-5.5); heuristic MIDI-to-Strudel converter
effect_target_headline: Rubric 0.74 for Qwen3-8B + SFT+RL (ours) vs 0.58 (+ SFT), 0.33 (Qwen3-8B) and 0.39 (GPT-5.5) on STRUDEL-SYNTH; 0.61 vs 0.54 (+ SFT) and 0.29 (GPT-5.5) on LMD
effect_correctness_headline: compared with the best frontier LLM, DECOMPOSER (8B) improves Onset F1 by +0.16 on STRUDEL-SYNTH and by +0.32 on LMD (Onset F1 0.73 and 0.60)
artifact_url: yewon-kim.com/decomposer (project page; STRUDEL-SYNTH stated as released)
notes: Eligibility borderline: generated artifact is a music DSL program (Strudel), not conventional production code; reviewer should confirm scope. Readability is evaluated with the same LLM judge and rubric used as the RL reward (risk of reward overfitting); no human validation or judge agreement reported. The LLM reranker Rank is mixed: for 8B on LMD, SFT+RL ranks 4.12 vs 4.01 for SFT only, and it is only comparable to frontier LLMs. Readability trades off with faithfulness (weight sweep, Fig. 4). Single run per setting, no variance. Compute only as training wall-clock (SFT about 1.5 h, RL about 8 days on 8xH100). No threats-to-validity section, only a short limitations paragraph. Tables are extracted column-wise but readable.

title: Hawk: Harnessing Hardware-Aware Knowledge for High-Performance NPU Kernel Generation
technique_name: Hawk (run-time hardware-aware knowledge synthesis with a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation + bottleneck-aware 2D retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion + effect-driven LLM knowledge distillation, inside an iterative compile/execute feedback agent)
metrics: efficiency: Speedup = L_std / L_opt against the CANNBench standard implementation, averaged over 20 test cases, and Performance Rate PR = (L_std - L_hw) / ((L_opt - L_hw) + (L_std - L_hw)) against the hardware theoretical lower bound, folded into an official Score = 20xCS + 30xAcc + 50xPR out of 100 [execution]; raw latency in ms [execution]. correctness: Compilation Success (CS, binary) and Acc (percentage of the 20 per-operator test cases passed) [execution]. Motivation study additionally uses Comp@1 and Pass@1 on MultiKernelBench.
benchmarks: CANNBench L1 kernels (8 operators shown: exp, foreach_addcdiv_scalar, foreach_norm, gelu, masked_scale, mish, sigmoid, swi_glu) and L2 kernels (16 complex operators), 20 test cases per Ascend C operator; motivation study uses 15 activation kernels and 17 matmul kernels from MultiKernelBench; knowledge base bootstrapped from 158 distilled entries mined from ops-nn (2,690 kernel files), strictly disjoint from the test-set categories.
models: GLM-5.1 (main backbone for Claude Code; closed/proprietary, reasoning); DeepSeek-V4-Flash (weaker backbone, generalization check); motivation study: DeepSeek-V4 Pro and GLM-4.5; Qwen3-Embedding-8B (8B, open) as the retrieval embedder.
baselines: Vanilla LLM (bare Claude Code); Few-Shot (Claude Code with a semantically retrieved reference kernel, target operator excluded from the corpus); CANNBot (base plugin with standard tools and official manuals) as the strongest/SOTA baseline; the CANNBench standard implementation as the speedup reference. Ablations: w/o Structured Representation, w/o 2D-Retrieval, w/o Distillation.
effect_target_headline: "Hawk elevates generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%, while achieving up to a 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines" (abstract); "it achieves a higher average Acc (0.80) and a faster average execution Speedup (1.34x) across the evaluated L1 operators, significantly outperforming the strongest baseline, CANNBot (0.49 Acc and 0.86x Speedup)"; per-operator "Speedups (averaging 2.10x and 2.39x over 20 test cases, respectively)" on exp and foreach_addcdiv_scalar; L2 kernels "achieved speedups up to 3.5x"; weaker backbone DeepSeek-V4-Flash "improved the average Speedup from 0.53x to 1.35x".
effect_correctness_headline: "elevates generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%" (average Acc 0.80 vs CANNBot 0.49 on L1); "100% on exp and foreach_addcdiv_scalar"; L2: "CANNBot yielded 0% Acc on 12 out of 16 operators. In contrast, Hawk delivered substantial functional improvements on 8 operators (e.g., 65% Acc on gcd)"; DeepSeek-V4-Flash "elevated the average Acc from 44.4% to 93.1%".
notes: All result figures (Figs. 6-12) are bar charts whose axis labels and values were destroyed by PDF extraction, so the per-operator numbers above come only from the prose; a human should verify them against the original PDF. Several internal inconsistencies worth checking: (a) the abstract and conclusion claim 'up to 2.2x speedup over SOTA' while the text reports average Speedup 1.34x vs CANNBot 0.86x; (b) the headline accuracy is 80.0% / 0.80 in the abstract and RQ1 but the ablation Table VI lists Hawk-Full Acc as 0.84 with Speedup normalized to 1.00x; (c) the RQ3 summary says the weaker DeepSeek backbone went from 15% to 60% Acc and 0.2x to 0.8x Speedup, while the body text of the same subsection says 44.4% to 93.1% Acc and 0.53x to 1.35x Speedup; (d) the Top-K discussion says 'K=6 yields marginal gains (+2% over K=6)', an apparent typo. CANNBench is used as the benchmark but no citation or task count for its L1 set is given beyond the 8 operators plotted. No artifact/code URL for Hawk itself is provided (only the third-party ops-nn and cannbot-skills repositories). No repeated runs or statistical tests; results appear to be single runs averaged over the 20 per-operator test cases.

title: TRIM: Reducing AI-Generated CodeSlop via Agent Trajectory Minimization
technique_name: TRIM (Trajectory-guided Redundancy Identification and Minimization), hierarchical counterfactual patch minimization over agent repair trajectories (TRIM-G and TRIM-NG variants)
metrics: readability-maintainability: Delta Slop % = normalized reduction in patch length (modified lines), edits/hunks removed [tool-static]; verbosity removed per SlopCodeBench definition [tool-static]; correctness: Live-kBench oracle = crash-reproducing script + Gemini-3-Flash LLM judge of semantic equivalence to developer patch (9 judgments, majority vote) [execution + llm-judge]; SWE-Bench hidden fail-to-pass tests [execution]; cost = number of test-suite executions
benchmarks: Live-kBench (534 Linux kernel vulnerabilities; 433 repaired, 293 non-trivial evaluated); SWE-Bench-Verified (333 SWE-agent Claude-Sonnet-4 trajectories); 4,544 repair trajectories total
models: Gemini-3-Pro (closed); Claude-Opus-4.5 (closed); Claude-Sonnet-4 (closed); Gemini-3-Flash (closed, minimization baseline and judge); Claude Sonnet 4.6 (closed, minimization baseline)
baselines: Agentic minimization with mini-SWE-agent (Only Diff, Only Traj, Both prompts; Gemini-3-Flash and Sonnet 4.6); DD-Hunk (Delta Debugging adapted to patch hunks); original agent patch
effect_target_headline: TRIM cuts CODESLOP by 17.9%–32.9% across agentic scaffolds (Live-kBench, TRIM-G edit level); 1.6×–3.1× improvement over agentic minimization; 20.0% ∆Slop on SWE-Bench-Verified (modified files); 66% of AP-introduced verbosity removed
effect_correctness_headline: TRIM preserves oracle correctness for 327/330 (99.1%) successful repairs (SWE-Bench-Verified); Live-kBench CrashFixer 22.47% -> 23.41% (+0.94), OpenHands -1.13 under full minimization
notes: Technique is a deterministic post-processing algorithm (not an LLM call) applied to LLM-agent patches; eligibility hinges on accepting patch minimization of LLM-generated code as an NF (maintainability/redundancy) intervention. CodeSlop is a functional-redundancy (patch-length) metric defined by the authors, not an established maintainability metric; verbosity measured via SlopCodeBench definition. Live-kBench is a 'live' recent-bug benchmark (partial contamination handling). Statistical test only vs DD-Hunk (p = 0.50, 95% CI). Abstract says 17.9% while intro says 17.8%. Tables partially garbled. No artifact URL.

title: Compiler-Grounded Hierarchical Diagnosis for LLM-Based Triton Kernel Optimization
technique_name: Compiler-grounded hierarchical diagnosis loop (pattern triage -> profiling diagnosis -> IR attribution -> compiler-source escalation -> evidence-backed source rewrite), with retrospective cross-operator pattern synthesis
metrics: efficiency: kernel execution speedup (initial Triton vs optimized Triton), geometric mean and median over operators, plus geometric-mean kernel time in microseconds [execution]; separate post-hoc speedup vs Torch NPU [execution]; correctness: validation/correctness test cases passed [execution]
benchmarks: NPUKernelBench-derived Ascend 950 suite (ported from KernelBench); 37 successfully converted Triton operators, 5 sampled cases each = 185 benchmark cases; Torch NPU comparison on 35 operators / 1678 cases
models: DeepSeek V4 Pro (closed/API, reasoning) driving an OpenCode agent
baselines: The initial (AI-converted) Triton kernel before optimization; separate post-optimization comparison against Torch NPU implementations
effect_target_headline: geometric-mean speedup of 4.35× and a median speedup of 2.73× from the initial to optimized Triton kernel; 22/37 exceed 2× and 13/37 exceed 5× (37 operators, NPUKernelBench-derived Ascend 950)
notes: System name is anonymized throughout ('the system'). No ablation: authors explicitly state no causal isolation of the four evidence levels, no profiling-only or always-deep control, and no token cost or wall-clock reporting. Correctness is used as a validation gate (e.g., 'passes all 50 correctness cases' for one example) but no aggregate correctness number is reported. Only one agent model evaluated, not justified. Several tables/figures garbled in PDF extraction (Figures 3-5, Table 1/2 numbers partially interleaved with text).

title: ARES: Adaptive Reasoning-Effort Steering for PPA- and Cost-Aware RTL Optimization with LLM Agents
technique_name: Ares adaptive reasoning-effort steering (patience counter escalating medium->high effort) in an edit-synthesize-measure agent loop with long-term markdown memory
metrics: efficiency: FoM = normalized area x power x delay after synthesis (Synopsys DC / PrimeTime) [tool-static]; cost: normalized dollar cost in high-calls
benchmarks: 24 open-source RTL modules (19 Dr. RTL designs, 2 RTLRewriter, 3 OpenCores); 21 training, 3 held-out test (tv80, uart, controller); plus MX multiply-accumulate unit drafted by Claude Opus 4.6
models: Claude Opus 4.6 (closed, reasoning, via Claude Code)
baselines: fixed low/medium/high reasoning effort; memoryless vs baseline vs engineered long-term memory; REvolution; Dr. RTL; hand-optimized MX_fp32
effect_target_headline: the effort policy lowers the FoM by 23–27% where the best fixed effort reaches 16–23%, at equal normalized cost (three held-out test designs); controller: Ares 0.694 vs REvolution 0.943 and Dr. RTL 0.923
notes: Eligibility borderline: task is LLM optimization (editing) of existing RTL, mostly human-written open-source designs, so a reviewer may classify as adjacent (EC4); one case optimizes an LLM-drafted MAC. Efficiency = hardware PPA, not software runtime/memory. Functional equivalence is enforced as an acceptance gate (testbench + JasperGold), not reported as an outcome. Single closed model; repeated runs (3 per config, 6 on MX MAC with std). Code promised upon publication. No threats-to-validity section. Figures/Table 1 garbled in extraction.

title: From C to Idiomatic Rust: A Ship-of-Theseus Agentic Translation
technique_name: Ship-of-Theseus agentic C-to-Rust migration: c2rust lossless baseline, leaf-first call-graph ordering, per-function LLM reimplementation, two hard gates (Gate A compilation plus idiomaticity criteria, Gate B runtime behavioural equivalence with trace-divergence feedback), split into Phase 1 (signatures and bodies) and Phase 2 (global mutable state)
metrics: security (memory safety): SAFE% = 100(1 - (EX+NM)/(EX0+NM0)) where EX counts unsafe extern "C" fn declarations and NM counts #[no_mangle] annotations; RUST% = 100(1 - (PA+DU)/(PA0+DU0)) where PA counts raw pointer arithmetic sites and DU counts deep unsafe operations such as copy_nonoverlapping and write_bytes; also absolute counts of static mut globals wrapped and of unsafe blocks [all tool-static source counting]. readability-maintainability (idiomaticity): the five criteria C1 zero unsafe in function signatures, C2 slice-based buffer access, C3 no static mut, C4 no extern "C" on internal functions, C5 no C string or memory functions, enforced as hard errors at Gate A [tool-static]; SLOC of the resulting codebase. Correctness: compilation plus end-to-end behavioural equivalence (same output and state modification for the same input), checked after every port [execution]
benchmarks: Single case study, no benchmark suite: iodine, a production-quality DNS tunnel of approximately 12.5 kSLOC of C across 17 source files, with 168 functions ported and 37 static mut globals (16 client, 21 server). c2rust baseline counts: 178 EX, 73 NM, 319 PA, 144 DU
models: Not properly reported. The paper states translation was performed 'using subscription-based plans and the OpenCode-based infrastructure' and that 'the best result (fewest iterations) was achieved with Qwen3.6-27B'; no other model is named, no sizes or open/closed status for the others, and no per-model results are given. ChatGPT and Copilot are acknowledged only for proofreading the manuscript
baselines: The c2rust transpiler output (mechanically translated, non-idiomatic Rust) serves as the baseline against which SAFE% and RUST% are defined. No comparison against direct LLM C-to-Rust translation (the approach the paper argues against) and no comparison against other migration tools
effect_target_headline: Server porting (commits 1-31) lifts SAFE% to 72% and RUST% to 47%; client porting (commits 32-41) completes all 168 signatures at SAFE%=95%; static-mut elimination (commits 39-45, extending to the end of history) wraps the 37 static mut globals (16 client, 21 server) in atomics or mutexes, lifting RUST% to its final 57%. The final codebase is approximately 10.3 kSLOC of idiomatic Rust across 16 files, translated from an original 12.5 kSLOC C codebase, with no unsafe extern "C" function declarations and no static mut left in the evaluated code. Client porting and static-mut elimination cut the client's unsafe blocks from roughly 86 to 40. Residual gap: five signal-handler EX type aliases and six #[no_mangle] entry-point annotations, and 99 PA and 99 DU uses confined to FFI boundary adapters
effect_correctness_headline: Functional equivalence was verified end-to-end: after each of the 168 function ports and each of the 37 static mut wrappings (16 client, 21 server), Gate B ran the tunnel against the public resolver under real traffic for 30 s or more, verified curl download and netperf through the tunnel, and passed a wire-format integration test
notes: ELIGIBILITY NOTE: this is a translation/migration paper, so a reviewer could route it to the 'adjacent' side list (LLM refactoring of human-written code, EC4). It was included because the evaluated artifact is new Rust code that the LLM wrote (from a C source and a transpiled baseline), the five idiomaticity criteria and the safety counts are explicitly non-functional properties of that generated code, and the technique is an intervention (an agentic compile-plus-runtime feedback loop) designed to improve them. Other caveats. (1) The models are essentially unreported: only Qwen3.6-27B is named, as the one needing fewest iterations, and the claim that 'a particular model choice does not materially affect the outcome' is asserted without any supporting data. The agent tooling 'rtk' and 'OAC' is named but never explained or cited. (2) Single case study on one 12.5 kSLOC program; no repeated runs, no variance, no statistical test, and no comparison against the direct-LLM-translation baseline the paper argues against. (3) SAFE% and RUST% are author-defined composite metrics; they deliberately omit the raw unsafe count (justified as not penalising correct refactoring), and the headline 'no unsafe extern "C" function declarations' sits slightly in tension with SAFE% = 95% (the residual is five signal-handler EX type aliases plus six #[no_mangle] annotations). (4) Correctness is verified thoroughly but qualitatively; no pass rate or test-count figure is given, and the runtime oracle depends on a live public DNS resolver, which is not a reproducible test environment. (5) Notable negative finding worth recording: batching three Mutex wrappings produced a live deadlock that compiled and passed static checks but stalled transfers at zero bytes, and POSIX getopt() externs (optarg, optind, opterr, optopt) were found to be unwrappable and were deferred. (6) The process is explicitly human-in-the-loop: type deduplication, FFI adapter scaffolding and lock-wrapping orchestration were handled by a human as exceptions, so the 37 developer-hours figure mixes agent and human effort. (7) No artifact release; the only URL is upstream iodine (https://code.kryo.se/iodine/). (8) No contamination discussion, despite iodine being a long-standing public open-source project. (9) Figures 1, 2 and 3 extracted poorly (the three-column code listing in Figure 1 and the metric plot in Figure 3 are interleaved), but all quoted numbers come from the running text of Section 4.3 and the Validation paragraph.

title: FABRICA: Agentic CUDA-to-CSL Translation and Optimization for Wafer-Scale Systems
technique_name: FABRICA: six-stage role-specialized agentic workflow (analyst, architect, implementer, reviewer, optimizer plus reference-isolation firewall) with retrieval from a consolidated Cerebras knowledge base, starter templates, failure-classified execution repair, and correctness-gated cycle optimization (an edit is accepted only if it stays valid and reduces median device cycles)
metrics: efficiency: in-kernel device cycle count and geometric-mean speedup over the same-target expert CSL reference, measured on the SDK fabric simulator and on WSE-3 hardware [execution]; correctness: bundle pass rate (compile + run + host/device contract preservation + valid timing path + numerical agreement on visible and held-out inputs), with six integrity checks against reference leakage and disabled timers [execution]
benchmarks: FABRICA-BENCH, introduced here: 49 paired CUDA/CSL tasks across four construction levels; a frozen 28-task Level 1-3 core set; an 8-task diagnostic set (5 runs each); a 15-task knowledge panel; a 12-task cross-model probe; 14 references for the optimization-only study; 35 bundles in the hardware-replay set (27 timing-comparable pairs)
models: Claude Opus 4.8 (closed, primary); Claude Sonnet 4.6 (closed); Claude Opus 4.6 (closed); gpt-oss-120b (open-weight); Gemma 4 31B (open-weight); gpt-oss-20b (open-weight); five further open-weight models on the probe; Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B used in the LoRA SFT pilot
baselines: Single-attempt generation with retrieval, review, repair and optimization disabled; expert-written CSL reference implementations in the benchmark bundles; ablation modes A (unguided), B (+classified execution repair), C (A + design records), D (B + design records), T (B + starting template); knowledge tiers (full knowledge / no retrieved Cerebras material / also no CSL primer)
effect_target_headline: For 27 generated/reference pairs with device-internal timing, geometric-mean speedup is 3.75x on the SDK simulator and 3.47x on WSE-3 hardware; by level on WSE-3: Level 1 7.49x, Level 2 2.56x, Level 3 2.71x, Level 4 1.24x; the optimization-only study improves all 14 measured references with a 1.44x geometric-mean speedup and seven programs improving by at least 25%
effect_correctness_headline: On a fixed 28-task Level 1-3 core comparison with Claude Opus 4.8, FABRICA raises success from 6/28 to 26/28; across the 49-task coverage evaluation, 38 tasks produce a correct program; the final three tasks are evaluated over three seeds and pass 8/9 runs; retrieved Cerebras knowledge separately raises success from 1/15 to 7/15
notes: Contamination and leakage are handled unusually carefully: a reference-isolation firewall, held-out inputs and seeds, six integrity checks, disjoint train/test splits, GEMM and GEMV held train-only because retrieved WaferLLM patterns overlap those families, and benchmark-disjoint filtering for the SFT pilot. The paper also contains a secondary training-time contribution (LoRA SFT on 6,066 harvested CUDA-to-CSL records for Qwen3-8B/14B) but reports only SDK-free structural proxy metrics (usable/contract/chrF/CSL vocabulary), not executable correctness or efficiency, so it is not recorded as a separate technique. 'Full prompts, candidates, checks, and measurements remain in the artifact' but no artifact URL is printed in the text. Attempt budgets are reported per study; no token, dollar or wall-clock cost is given. Figures 5-8 and several tables are garbled in PDF extraction (axis labels split per character); headline numbers were taken from the abstract, Section V and the conclusion.

title: Argus: Orchestrating Cross-Layer GPU Performance Measurements around Semantic Regions

metrics: efficiency: best-found speedup over original kernel, geometric-mean speedup, count of instances improved / >=10% speedup, best-so-far speedup vs trials, per-token decode latency (ms/token) with device-side timestamps [execution]
benchmarks: 44 Triton kernel instances from 10 kernel families (8 warp-specialized persistent GEMM configurations + 9 attention variants x 4 block sizes); one representative Triton kernel across 5 agent workflows; persistent TinyLlama-1.1B batch-1 decode megakernel; cross-level PGO on 4 GEMM shapes x 5 2/4-GPU settings (no LLM)

Correctness is only a gate (Triton compile + numerical equivalence), no correctness rates reported. Compute reporting is a fixed 25-trial budget plus profiling overhead (not LLM tokens/cost). Single run per configuration, no variance. Cross-level PGO (7% throughput) uses an analytic model without an LLM and should not count toward the technique effect. No threats-to-validity or limitations section; no code URL. Agent workflows were reproduced by the authors, not original implementations. Figures 4-6, 8-13 partly garbled.

title: ForgeMegakernel: A General Framework for Efficient Auto-Regressive Model Decode Megakernels
technique_name: ForgeMegakernel (ten-milestone knowledge base + mid-state test oracle + fresh-context agent loop with GPU measurement and reviewer agent)
metrics: efficiency: model bandwidth utilization (MBU %) from host-derived byte count and two-point-slope latency, per-token latency (us/tok), speedup vs baselines [execution; profiler]; correctness: mean |delta log p| vs float64 forward pass, GSM8K answer accuracy inside SGLang, functional checks [execution]
benchmarks: 14 decode cells (model, batch, sequence length) across eight model families (Llama-3.2-1B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-2-13B-chat, Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B/4B/8B, Qwen2.5-3B, MiniCPM4-0.5B/1B/3B, MiniCPM5-1B, NanBeige4-3B); GSM8K 200 test questions for serving evaluation

notes: Domain is GPU kernel generation for LLM inference; the NF dimension is efficiency of agent-written CUDA. No-technique (naive-prompt agent) comparison is only in the motivating Observations on five cells (geomean 0.75x SGLang utilization); main results compare to engines/compiler. Milestone ablation is one campaign on one cell. Figures/tables (Fig. 3, Tables 2-3) are garbled in extraction. No code URL given. Only one GPU architecture; limitations section is brief.

title: FlashVector: Agent for Hierarchical Model Serving Stack Optimization
technique_name: FlashVector (layer-agent abstraction with a knowledge base and a Profile-Diagnose-Optimize-Verify loop plus a post-run Refine stage; optimize locally, verify globally; always-on self-retriggering loop)
metrics: efficiency: latency speedup and throughput increase versus the production baseline; sustained requests per second per pod at a fixed latency SLO; p99 latency in ms; per-kernel latency in microseconds; percentage of GPU time and dispatcher overhead; per-call-site kernel speedup factors [all execution]. Correctness: element-wise output comparison against recorded baseline predictions, with class-dependent bars (bit-exact for deterministic rewrites; 1e-3 element-wise absolute deviation with at most 0.1% of elements beyond it for floating-point reordering, 1e-4 for FP32 serving; business metrics for intentional approximations; shadow-traffic canary for configuration changes) [execution]
benchmarks: No public benchmark; evaluated in situ on Unity's Vector advertising platform. Table 1 reports 6 production models (Retrieval model, Ranking models 1-4, Gamer model); Table 3 reports one preprocessor service across 3 cumulative optimization stages; Table 4 reports 4 production models (A-D) for configuration tuning; Table 2 reports 5 Cython kernel replacements
models: Not reported anywhere in the paper; the underlying LLM powering the agents is never named
baselines: Existing hand-tuned production stack: for Case 2 an AOT-compiled (PyTorch AOTInductor), FP16-quantized model on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU with batch size 2000; for Case 3 a 940 RPS/pod preprocessor baseline; for Case 4 a hand-tuned configuration left at the framework default batch size with utilization-target scaling
effect_target_headline: FlashVector achieved up to 2x throughput increase and up to 1.98x latency speedup on model server, and up to 1.6x throughput increase on feature store. Case 1: speed up to 30x on the Triton input-conversion step. Case 2: attention latency cut from 996.5 microseconds to 279.8 microseconds (a 3.56x speedup); embedding changes reduce total GPU kernel time by 33.4%, cut forward-pass latency by 30.1%, and lower dispatcher overhead from 44.8% to 28.5%. Case 3: 940 requests per second at baseline, roughly 1.5k with all three in place, a 1.6x improvement
effect_correctness_headline: Because the fused kernel preserves the original operation order and accumulation precision, it generates attention weights that are bit-identical to the baseline, which we verify by element-wise comparison
notes: ELIGIBILITY IS BORDERLINE and a human reviewer should confirm the call. The system optimizes an existing, human-written production codebase (NVIDIA Triton C++, a Python feature-processing service, PyTorch model code) rather than generating programs from a specification, which looks like the 'adjacent' side list (LLM refactoring of human-written code / EC4). It was included because IC2 explicitly admits code 'edited by an LLM', EC4 requires 'no LLM generation', and the agent does write new code (a fused CUDA kernel, hand-written Cython kernels, a C++ rewrite of a deserialization path). Flip to exclude/EC4/adjacent if the review intends EC4 to cover LLM-driven optimization of existing code. Other issues: (1) The underlying LLM is NEVER named anywhere in the paper, so QA5 is 0 and reimplementation is not possible. (2) This is an industrial experience report of case studies, not a controlled evaluation: there is no ablation, no public benchmark, no artifact release, and no threats-to-validity section. (3) The agent's correctness verification is well specified (bit-exactness and tolerance bars per change class) but no aggregate correctness results are reported. (4) Measurement noise is handled rigorously (noise floor estimated from repeated no-op baseline runs, re-measurement at larger sample sizes), which is the strongest methodological element. (5) Tables 1-4 are garbled by PDF extraction: Table 1's column values are split from the model names, Table 2's left column (Python functions replaced) is separated from its speedup column, and Table 4's header row is interleaved; the mappings are recoverable but should be re-checked against the original. (6) Figures 2-6 are referenced but their content is not in the extracted text. (7) Section 5.2 text appears out of order in the extraction (Case 3 baseline setup text is interleaved into Case 2). (8) The only URL given is a GitHub issue for a contributed upstream fix (https://github.com/triton-inference-server/server/issues/8348), not a research artifact.

title: Can Agents Design Better Chips with a Higher Level Abstraction?

benchmarks: 11-task suite (LLM decode attention, norm+quant+linear, INT8 GEMM in 2 variants, BM25 gather, paged-KV compact, LServe page select, NMS, PointPillars encoder, stereo SAD, StreamHLS GEMM and depthwise conv)

notes: Artifact is hardware design code (HLS C++/Verilog) evaluated for latency and area; reviewers should confirm hardware code counts as production code. Each experiment run once; geometric means exclude pairs with invalid Direct RTL baselines (n=15/13). Validity (correctness) shown only as invalid markers per task, not as rates. Also evaluates Post-Compiler HLS Refinement (up to 3.3x over StreamHLS on SHL2). Compute reported only as time budgets. Authors note prompt sensitivity. Figures partially garbled.

title: TicTacBench: Benchmarking Timing Closure Capabilities of Coding Agents
technique_name: TicTacSkill: agent skill encoding timing-closure Standard Operating Procedures (critical-path localization, datapath/pipeline/control design checks, evidence-driven search, pre/post-PnR mismatch handling) derived from trajectory failure analysis, given to the coding agent before solving
metrics: efficiency: post-PnR Timing Closure Rate, Avg. delta WNS%, Avg. delta EDDP% (energy-delay-squared product), Avg. delta ADP% (area-delay product), cell count, power [tool-static, post-PnR STA]; correctness: compile, synthesizability and formal equivalence check as gate [tool-static]

effect_target_headline: The GPT-5.4-based agent improves from 53.3% to 56.7% Timing Closure Rate and from 48.7% to 66.4% Avg. ∆ WNS%. The MiniMax M2.7-based agent ... increasing from 23.3% to 36.7%; DeepSeek V4 Flash-based agent improves from 33.3% to 43.3%
notes: Primarily a benchmark paper; the technique (TicTacSkill) ablation is on 3 models, single run each, no statistics. Within efficiency, timing improved but area-delay product worsened for GPT-5.4 (-2.5% to -3.6%) and MiniMax (-9.6% to -10.9%), and MiniMax EDDP worsened (-0.7% to -7.2%). Table IV label 'DeepSeek' is called DeepSeek V4 Flash in text, but its w/o-skill numbers may not match the leaderboard figure (garbled); check. Failure taxonomy derived using an LLM analyst (DeepSeek V4 Flash). Correctness is only an equivalence-check gate, not reported as a rate. Input RTL is human-written suboptimal designs (EC4/adjacent borderline). Limitations section brief.

title: ChipMEM: Verification-Grounded Memory for EDA Agents
technique_name: ChipMEM (verification-gated procedural skill memory retrieved by RTL embedding similarity + hierarchical Beta statistical memory for tool retry/recovery advice)
metrics: efficiency: mean area improvement (%), power improvement (%), timing/WNS/TNS change, cell/wire ratio after synthesis [execution/tool synthesis measurements]; correctness: functional equivalence pass rate, strict gate pass rate, CVDP hidden-test pass rate [execution/formal]
benchmarks: RTL-OPT (38 designs); RTLRewriter-Bench (59 cases: 54 short, 5 long; 54 scored); custom open-source design set (20 designs); OpenTitan (10 IP blocks x 5 attempts); held-out cohorts A (20) and B (16); CVDP CID012/CID013 (40 testbench tasks); SWE-bench Pro pilot (100 tasks)
models: GPT-5.5, size NR, closed, reasoning (medium); Qwen3.8-27B, 27B, open, NR

notes: Domain is hardware RTL PPA (area/power/timing) rather than software runtime; reviewer should confirm RTL PPA counts as efficiency. CVDP testbench part is test code (EC3-type) and not used for the NF outcome. GPT-5.5 experiments run on proprietary Cadence ChipStack 2.0 agent (limits reimplementation). RTL-OPT ChipMEM result selects best valid result across three result sets (favourable selection). Custom-design Pass@k is lower with ChipMEM (80% vs 85% at Pass@5). Appendix notes the legacy OpenTitan run mined skills after every session including failures, not the PASS-only rule. Held-out transfer only on CVDP (testbench) tasks with frozen memory; held-out PPA cohorts had no memory-off comparison. Mean ± std and bootstrap CIs for cost; no significance tests on PPA. Tables garbled but recoverable. Dated year 2026 (arXiv 2609.27067).

title: KernelOPT: Dispatch-Aware Agentic Search for GPU Kernel Optimization
technique_name: KernelOPT (Inductor-aware synthesis + profiling-guided multi-agent beam search with experience memory and four-gate verification)
metrics: efficiency: end-to-end wall-clock speedup vs torch.compile and eager (geometric mean, optimized/matched/fallback counts), sub-kernel NCU duration, occupancy, registers [execution]; correctness: multi-seed allclose vs eager PyTorch (1e-3 per candidate, 1e-4 final) and float64 error-ratio check [execution]
benchmarks: KernelBench, all 250 problems (Level 1: 100, Level 2: 100, Level 3: 50); plus 10 Triton and 10 Helion tutorial kernels; ablations on 50-problem stratified subset
models: Claude Sonnet 4.6, size NR, closed, instruct
baselines: torch.compile (Inductor max-autotune), eager PyTorch; KernelAgent replicated on KernelBench L1 with same hardware and backend; ablations (no beam, no NCU profiling, no memory, T=1, no perf gate, no Inductor-aware filtering)
effect_target_headline: geometric mean speedups over torch.compile of 1.40× (L1), 1.15× (L2), and 1.07× (L3) across all kernels, including fallback cases; Optimized-only geomeans 2.54× (L1: 36/100), 1.84× (L2: 23/100), and 1.37× (L3: 11/50); vs KernelAgent on L1: 1.649× vs 0.966× geomean

notes: Single LLM (Claude Sonnet 4.6), single run per problem; ablation differences tested with Fisher's exact test (p<0.01). Compute reported as ~1,100 H200 GPU-hours and ~60K tokens per NCU prompt; no per-run LLM call/token totals. Fallbacks preserve compiler baseline, so all-problem geomeans include 1.00x fallbacks. No dedicated threats section, but implementation limitations and unestablished claims (accepted-side rho) are discussed. Per-kernel Table 10 and several tables are garbled in extraction. KernelBench contamination not discussed.

title: Groupwise Agentic Grading and Advantage Redistribution for Code Agent RL
technique_name: Gagar (Groupwise Agentic Grading for Advantage Redistribution): an SFT-trained agentic grader ranks test-passing rollouts in a shared workspace on five code-quality criteria, and the resulting quality factors drive sum-preserving rescaling of positive advantages in GRPO-style code-agent RL
metrics: readability-maintainability: rubric-weighted quality score W = 0.30*approach suitability + 0.25*implementation precision + 0.20*minimality of changes + 0.15*unintended side effects + 0.10*codebase consistency, each scored 1 to 5 [llm-judge]; average win rate among test-passing candidates from joint groupwise rankings [llm-judge]; share of groups ranked first with ties split equally [llm-judge]; fraction of candidates in the highest quality tier T1 [llm-judge]. Correctness: avg@3 pass rate on DeepSWE v1.1 and SWE-bench Pro [execution]. Agent process cost (not code efficiency): mean main-agent interaction turns and mean total token length [execution]. Training diagnostics: policy entropy, policy-gradient loss, mean training-rollout length
benchmarks: DeepSWE v1.1 (long-horizon software development) and SWE-bench Pro (repository-level issue resolution); avg@3 with three samples per task. The implementation-quality evaluation uses a fixed random sample of 30 DeepSWE tasks, pooling up to three rollouts per method per task with anonymized identifiers and randomized order. Task counts for the full benchmarks are not stated
models: Policy models: MiMo-V2.6-Flash, 310B total / 15B active parameters, mixture-of-experts, proprietary (Xiaomi), initialized from a pre-RL SFT checkpoint; MiMo-V2.6-Pro, 1.02T total / 42B active parameters, mixture-of-experts, proprietary, likewise from a pre-RL SFT checkpoint. Online grader: the pre-RL SFT checkpoint of MiMo-V2.6-Pro (initially Claude Opus 5). Offline quality judge: Claude Opus 5, closed. External comparison models: Kimi K3 (2.8T), GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5
baselines: Binary-outcome reward RL without online quality grading, trained under identical settings and compared at shared steps; a downweighting-only ablation that applies quality factors without restoring removed positive credit or re-centering; external frontier models K3, GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Opus 5 for the mixed-task runs
effect_target_headline: At the final shared checkpoint, Gagar achieves a mean quality score of 4.03 versus 3.70 for the baseline, with an average win rate of 69.8% among passing candidates. It ranks first in 65.0% of groups after splitting ties. Across the audited checkpoints, improvements are most apparent in implementation precision, minimality of changes, and avoidance of unintended side effects; the fraction of candidates assigned to the highest-quality tier, T1, increases from 25.4% to 34.3%
effect_correctness_headline: At step 28, Gagar achieves 62.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, exceeding the baseline by 12.1 percentage points (the baseline fell from 58.5% at step 20 to 50.2%). With continued training, Gagar reaches a peak DeepSWE pass rate of 63.4% at step 44. On SWE-bench Pro, the baseline plateaus at approximately 59% from step 16 through step 28, whereas Gagar reaches 62.5% at step 52. After mixed-task RL, DeepSWE v1.1 avg@3 reaches 67.9 (Flash) and 71.9 (Pro), with SWE-bench Pro at 60.9 and 62.7
notes: Scope note for the reviewer: the five graded criteria (approach suitability, implementation precision, minimality of changes, unintended side effects, codebase consistency) map to the readability-maintainability dimension, and the paper frames them as producing 'maintainable, merge-ready code' that reduces developer review effort. The reported turn-count and token-length reductions (e.g. DeepSWE mean turns 132.3 to 111.6 and mean tokens 191.9k to 172.9k at step 28) are the AGENT'S process cost, not the runtime efficiency of the generated code, so they are recorded under compute_reported rather than as an efficiency outcome; a reviewer who treats agent cost as efficiency would add that dimension. Other caveats: (1) The quality evaluation is an LLM judge (Claude Opus 5) on only 30 DeepSWE tasks with up to three rollouts per method; it is blinded (anonymized identifiers, randomized order) but there is no human validation, no inter-rater agreement, and no check against the judge's own self-preference, even though Claude Opus 5 is simultaneously an external comparison model in Table 1 and was the original online grader. (2) No limitations or threats-to-validity section, no contamination discussion, no artifact release. (3) Single training run per condition and no confidence intervals or significance tests; the comparison is complicated by the baseline being stopped early at step 28 because of degradation. (4) The models (MiMo-V2.6-Flash and Pro), the grader checkpoint and the SFT data for the grader are all proprietary and undescribed, so the grading component cannot be reproduced; the advantage-redistribution mathematics and all its constants are fully specified in Section 3.3 and Appendix A. (5) Figures 2, 3 and 4 are reduced to scattered axis numbers by PDF extraction, so all numbers above were taken from the running text, which states them explicitly; Tables 1 and 2 extracted cleanly. (6) The programming language of the benchmarks is never stated.
